chapters.n: John opens his Gospel by echoing Genesis 1. Before creation, Jesus already existed as “the Word” — the one through whom God speaks and acts. He was with God and was Himself divine. Latter-day Saints understand this as the premortal Jehovah.

f.g: Greek logos — speech, reason, message. Christ is God’s self-expression. JST John 1:1 reads “In the beginning was the gospel preached through the Son.”

chapters.n: John repeats for emphasis: from the very beginning, the Word was together with God the Father. The Son is distinct from the Father yet united with Him.

f.w: The same was in the beginning with God

chapters.n: Everything that exists was created through Him. Under the Father’s direction, the premortal Christ was the Creator of the earth and worlds without number.

f.w: All things were made by him

chapters.n: He is the source of all life, and that life is light for humanity — giving understanding, guidance, and hope.

f.w: the life was the light of men

chapters.n: His light shines into a dark world, and the darkness has neither understood it nor overcome it. Both meanings fit the Greek.

f.g: Greek katalambanō can mean “grasped/understood” or “overpowered/overcome.”

chapters.n: John the Baptist enters the story — a man sent by God with a mission. (The author of this Gospel is a different John, the Beloved Disciple.)

f.g: John the Baptist, the forerunner. His name means “Jehovah is gracious.”

chapters.n: John came as a witness to testify about the Light, so that everyone might believe through his testimony. Witness is a key word in this Gospel.

f.w: to bear witness of the Light

chapters.n: John was not the Light himself. Some followers of the Baptist may have exalted him too highly, so the author makes it clear.
Christ is the true Light who gives light to every person born into the world. Latter-day Saints call this the Light of Christ, given to all.
He came into the very world He made, yet the world did not recognize Him. Creation failed to know its Creator.
He came to His own covenant people, Israel, and as a whole they did not receive Him.
But everyone who did receive Him and believe in Him received power to become God’s children — not by birth but by covenant and spiritual rebirth.

f.w: power to become the sons of God

chapters.n: These are born not through human ancestry or human effort, but by God. Spiritual birth comes from Him.

f.g: Not through physical descent or lineage.

chapters.n: The heart of the Gospel: the eternal Word became a mortal man and lived among us. Eyewitnesses saw His glory — the glory of the Father’s Only Begotten Son, full of grace and truth.

f.g: Literally “pitched His tent” — recalling the tabernacle where God’s glory dwelt in Israel.

chapters.n: John the Baptist cried out: the one coming after me ranks above me, because He existed before me. Though Jesus was born after John, He was premortally first.

f.g: Ranks ahead of me, has a higher position.

chapters.n: From His fulness we all receive blessing upon blessing. Latter-day revelation adds that Christ Himself grew “from grace to grace” until He received a fulness.

f.g: Grace upon grace — one gift following another.

chapters.n: The law came through Moses, a gift that prepared Israel. Grace and truth in their fulness came through Jesus Christ, to whom the law pointed.

f.w: the law was given by Moses

chapters.n: No one has seen God the Father at any time — except, the JST adds, those who bear record of the Son. Jesus, close to the Father’s heart, has made Him known.

f.w: No man hath seen God at any time
f.g: JST John 1:19: “No man hath seen God at any time, except he hath borne record of the Son.”

f.w: in the bosom of the Father
f.g: In the closest intimacy with the Father.
Explained, revealed; Greek exēgeomai, root of “exegesis.”

chapters.n: Now John’s testimony is told. Religious authorities send priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask John the Baptist who he is.

f.g: In John’s Gospel often means the Jewish religious authorities, not the Jewish people as a whole.
Temple assistants from the tribe of Levi.

chapters.n: John declares plainly that he is not the Messiah. Many were wondering whether he was.
Are you Elijah? No. Are you “that prophet” Moses promised? No. The JST clarifies that John denied being the Elias who would restore all things, though he was an Elias, a forerunner.

f.g: Elijah; also a title for a forerunner or restorer. Jesus did say John was the Elias who was to come.

chapters.n: Frustrated, they press him: we need an answer for those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?

f.g: They need an official report for the Jerusalem leaders.

chapters.n: He answers with Isaiah: I am a voice crying in the wilderness — prepare the Lord’s road. He sees himself as only a voice; the message is about Another.

f.w: the voice of one crying in the wilderness

f.g: Greek form of Isaiah.

chapters.n: These messengers were from the Pharisees, the strict religious party.

f.g: A movement devoted to strict observance of the law and oral traditions.

chapters.n: They ask: then why are you baptizing, if you’re not the Messiah, Elijah, or the Prophet? Baptism suggested a new beginning only a figure of authority might start.

f.g: John’s baptism treated Jews as needing to repent and enter anew, like converts.

chapters.n: John says he baptizes only with water, but someone already standing among them, unrecognized, is far greater.
He comes after John but ranks ahead of him. John says he isn’t worthy even to untie His sandal strap — a slave’s task.

f.g: Sandal strap; untying sandals was a lowly servant’s duty.

chapters.n: This took place at Bethabara on the east side of the Jordan River, where John was baptizing.

f.g: “House of the crossing” — a ford of the Jordan; some manuscripts read “Bethany beyond Jordan.”

chapters.n: The next day John sees Jesus coming and proclaims: Look, the Lamb of God who takes away the world’s sin! Every Passover lamb and temple sacrifice pointed to Him.
This is the one I spoke of, John says — the man who comes after me but ranks before me, because He existed first.
John didn’t know Him as the Messiah at first, but his baptizing was meant to reveal Him to Israel.

f.g: Revealed, made known.

chapters.n: John testifies that he saw the Spirit come down from heaven in the form of a dove and remain on Jesus. Joseph Smith taught the dove was a sign; the Holy Ghost is a personage of spirit.
God had told John that the one on whom he saw the Spirit descend and remain would be the one who baptizes with the Holy Ghost.
John has seen it and testifies: this is the Son of God.

f.g: Testified, bore witness.

f.w: this is the Son of God

chapters.n: The next day John is standing with two of his own disciples.

f.g: One is Andrew (v. 40); the unnamed other is traditionally John, the author.

chapters.n: Watching Jesus walk by, John again says: Look, the Lamb of God!

f.g: A repeated testimony that turns his own followers toward Jesus.

chapters.n: Hearing this, the two disciples leave John and follow Jesus. John’s goal was to point people to Christ, not to keep them for himself.
Jesus turns and asks: What are you seeking? They respond, “Rabbi, where are you staying?” — they want to be with Him, not just to get an answer.

f.g: Jesus’ first words in John’s Gospel — a question for every reader.
Hebrew “my great one” — a respectful title for a teacher.

chapters.n: “Come and see,” He says. They go, see where He is staying, and spend the rest of the day with Him. It was about four in the afternoon — a time the eyewitness never forgot.

f.g: About 4 p.m., counting from sunrise.

chapters.n: One of the two was Andrew, brother of Simon Peter.

f.g: Greek for “manly.” In John’s Gospel he is often bringing others to Jesus.

chapters.n: The first thing Andrew does is find his brother Simon and tell him: We have found the Messiah!

f.g: Messiah — Hebrew for “anointed one,” the same as Greek Christos.

chapters.n: Andrew brings Simon to Jesus, who looks at him and gives him a new name: Cephas, meaning “stone” — Peter in Greek. Jesus sees what Simon will become. The JST adds that Cephas means “a seer, or a stone.”

f.g: Aramaic for “rock” or “stone”; Greek Petros. JST John 1:42: “which is by interpretation, a seer, or a stone.”
Jonah; elsewhere his father is called John.

chapters.n: The next day, as He sets out for Galilee, Jesus finds Philip and says, “Follow me.”
Philip is from Bethsaida, the hometown of Andrew and Peter, on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee.

f.g: “House of fishing.”

chapters.n: Philip finds Nathanael and announces: we have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about — Jesus of Nazareth, Joseph’s son.

f.g: “Gift of God”; often identified with Bartholomew in the other Gospels.

f.w: of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, did write

chapters.n: Nathanael is skeptical: can anything good come from Nazareth, a small, obscure village? Philip doesn’t argue; he simply says, “Come and see.”

f.g: A small Galilean village never mentioned in the Old Testament.

chapters.n: As Nathanael approaches, Jesus says: here is a true Israelite with no deceit in him — perhaps a contrast with Jacob, the original “Israel,” known for trickery.

f.g: Deceit, craftiness.

chapters.n: Surprised, Nathanael asks how Jesus knows him. Jesus says He saw him under the fig tree before Philip called him — a place where devout Jews often studied and prayed.

f.g: A symbol of peace and a common spot for meditation and study of the law.

chapters.n: Nathanael is won over: Rabbi, You are the Son of God, the King of Israel! Encountering Christ’s knowledge of him personally brings instant testimony.

f.w: thou art the Son of God

chapters.n: Jesus replies: you believe because I said I saw you under the fig tree? You will see much greater things.
He promises they will see heaven opened and angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man — recalling Jacob’s ladder. Jesus Himself is the connection between heaven and earth.

f.g: Hebrew “Amen, amen” — “Truly, truly,” a solemn affirmation used only in John.

f.w: angels of God ascending and descending

chapters.n: A few days after calling His first disciples, Jesus attends a wedding in Cana, a Galilean village near Nazareth. His mother Mary is there too, perhaps helping the family.

f.g: Probably counted from the last event in chapter 1.
A village a few miles north of Nazareth; Nathanael’s hometown.

chapters.n: Jesus and His new disciples have also been invited. His first miracle takes place at a joyful family celebration.

f.g: Invited.

chapters.n: The wine runs out — a serious embarrassment for the host family, since village weddings lasted up to a week and hospitality was a matter of honor. Mary turns to Jesus.

f.g: Ran short of wine.

chapters.n: Jesus’ reply sounds abrupt in English, but “Woman” was a respectful address. The JST renders it: “Woman, what wilt thou have me to do for thee? that will I do; for mine hour is not yet come.”

f.g: A polite, even honorable, form of address — Jesus uses it from the cross too.

f.w: mine hour is not yet come
f.g: His “hour” in John points to His death and glorification.

chapters.n: Mary’s faith is clear. She tells the servants: whatever He tells you, do it. That counsel still applies to every disciple.

f.w: Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it

chapters.n: Six large stone jars stand nearby, used for ritual hand-washing under Jewish purity customs. Each holds about twenty to thirty gallons.

f.g: Stone vessels were believed not to become ritually impure, unlike clay.
A measure of about 9–10 gallons; each jar held 20–30 gallons.

chapters.n: Jesus tells the servants to fill the jars with water, and they fill them to the very brim — leaving no room for anything to be added.

f.g: Completely full — no trickery possible.

chapters.n: He tells them to draw some out and take it to the master of the banquet, and they obey — trusting before seeing.

f.g: The head steward or master of ceremonies at the feast.

chapters.n: The banquet master tastes the water that has become wine. He doesn’t know where it came from, but the servants who obeyed do. He calls over the groom.

f.w: the servants which drew the water knew
f.g: Those who obey are often the first to witness God’s works.

chapters.n: He tells the groom: normally the best wine is served first and the cheaper wine later. But you’ve saved the best for last! Christ’s gifts surpass what came before.

f.g: Drunk freely.

f.w: thou hast kept the good wine until now
f.g: Many see a symbol: the new covenant surpasses the old.

chapters.n: This was the first of Jesus’ “signs,” revealing His glory, and His disciples believed in Him. John calls miracles “signs” because they point to who Jesus is.

f.g: Literally “beginning of signs” — John records seven signs.

chapters.n: Afterward, Jesus goes down to Capernaum on the Sea of Galilee with His mother, brothers, and disciples, staying a few days.

f.g: A lakeside town that became Jesus’ base in Galilee.

chapters.n: With Passover approaching, Jesus goes up to Jerusalem. John’s Gospel mentions three Passovers, which is why we think Jesus’ ministry lasted about three years.
In the temple courts He finds merchants selling cattle, sheep, and doves for sacrifice, and moneychangers at their tables. A place of prayer has become a bustling market.

f.g: They exchanged foreign coins for the Tyrian shekels required for the temple tax — often at a profit.

chapters.n: He makes a whip from cords and drives them out with their animals, scattering the money and overturning the tables. Only John places a cleansing at the start of the ministry; the other Gospels describe one in the final week.

f.g: A whip made of rushes or rope.

chapters.n: To the dove sellers He says: get these out of here! Don’t turn My Father’s house into a marketplace. Calling the temple “My Father’s house” is a bold claim to be God’s Son.
His disciples remember a line from the Psalms: zeal for God’s house will consume Him. His passion for the temple would indeed help lead to His death.

f.w: The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up

chapters.n: The authorities demand a miraculous sign to prove He has authority to do this.
Jesus answers cryptically: destroy this temple, and I will raise it up in three days. His sign will be His own resurrection.
They take Him literally. Herod’s rebuilding of the temple had been going on for forty-six years — how could He rebuild it in three days?

f.g: Herod began rebuilding about 20/19 BC, which helps date this event to about AD 27–28; work continued until AD 63.
Raise it up, build it.

chapters.n: John explains: He was speaking of the temple of His body. His body is the true dwelling place of God.
After the Resurrection, the disciples remembered this and believed both the scriptures and Jesus’ words. Some understanding comes only later.
During the Passover feast in Jerusalem, many believed in Him because of the miracles they saw.

f.g: Their belief was based on seeing signs — a beginning, but shallow.

chapters.n: But Jesus didn’t entrust Himself to them, because He knew everyone’s heart. Faith built only on wonders can be fickle.

f.g: Entrust Himself — same Greek word as “believed” in v. 23, a wordplay.

chapters.n: He needed no one to tell Him about people, for He knew what was in each person. Nothing is hidden from Him.

f.w: he knew what was in man

chapters.n: Nicodemus is a Pharisee and a member of the ruling council — a respected, learned leader. He appears three times in John, and his faith seems to grow each time.

f.g: A Greek name meaning “victor over the people.”
A member of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high council.

chapters.n: He comes at night — perhaps to avoid being seen, or simply for an uninterrupted conversation. He acknowledges that Jesus’ miracles show God is with Him.

f.g: In John, night often hints at spiritual darkness someone is coming out of.
A sincere but incomplete view of Jesus.

chapters.n: Jesus goes straight to the heart: unless a person is born again, they cannot see God’s kingdom. A fresh spiritual start is required, not just admiration.

f.g: Greek anōthen means both “again” and “from above.”

chapters.n: Nicodemus takes it literally: how can a grown man re-enter his mother’s womb? His question shows how foreign the idea of spiritual rebirth is to him.

f.g: Perhaps Nicodemus is also asking how an older man can truly change.

chapters.n: Jesus explains: one must be born of water and of the Spirit — baptism by immersion and the gift of the Holy Ghost — to enter God’s kingdom. Both ordinances are essential.

f.w: born of water and of the Spirit

chapters.n: Physical birth produces physical life; spiritual birth produces spiritual life. Each kind of birth brings its own kind of life.
Don’t be surprised, Jesus says, that I told you all must be born again. The “ye” is plural — this applies to everyone.

f.g: Don’t be amazed.

chapters.n: The wind blows wherever it wants; you hear it but can’t see where it comes from or goes. The Spirit works the same way — invisible, yet its effects are real.

f.g: In Greek (pneuma) and Hebrew (ruach), the same word means both “wind” and “spirit.”
Wishes, chooses.

chapters.n: Nicodemus is still puzzled: how can these things happen?
Jesus gently challenges him: you’re a respected teacher of Israel and don’t understand this? The prophets spoke of a new heart and spirit.

f.g: “The teacher of Israel” — a prominent religious instructor.

chapters.n: We speak about what we know and testify of what we have seen, Jesus says, yet you don’t accept our testimony.

f.w: We speak that we do know

chapters.n: If you don’t believe when I describe earthly things, like birth and wind, how will you believe heavenly realities?

f.g: Deeper truths about God and eternity.

chapters.n: No one has gone up to heaven except the one who came down from it — the Son of Man. Jesus speaks with firsthand knowledge of heaven.

f.w: he that came down from heaven

f.g: Missing in some early manuscripts.

chapters.n: When Israel was dying from snakebites, Moses raised a bronze serpent on a pole, and all who looked lived. So the Son of Man must be lifted up on the cross.

f.w: as Moses lifted up the serpent

chapters.n: ...so that everyone who believes in Him will have eternal life. As with the serpent, the cure is to look in faith.

f.g: In John, both a quality of life now and life with God forever.

chapters.n: Perhaps the most beloved verse in the Bible: God loved the world so much that He gave His Only Begotten Son, so that whoever believes in Him will not perish but have everlasting life.
God didn’t send His Son to condemn the world but to save it. Christ’s mission is rescue.

f.w: not his Son into the world to condemn the world

chapters.n: Whoever believes in Him escapes condemnation. Whoever refuses to believe stands condemned already — not because God rejects them, but because they reject the remedy.
Here is the judgment: the Light came into the world, but people preferred darkness because their actions were evil.

f.w: men loved darkness rather than light

chapters.n: Those who do evil hate the light and avoid it, so their actions won’t be exposed.

f.g: Exposed and shown to be wrong.

chapters.n: But those who live by the truth come to the light, gladly letting it show that their deeds were done through God.

f.g: Done in God’s strength and in harmony with Him.

f.w: he that doeth truth cometh to the light

chapters.n: Jesus and His disciples go out into the Judean countryside, where He spends time with them and baptizes. John 4:2 clarifies that His disciples performed the baptisms under His direction.

f.g: Stayed.

chapters.n: John the Baptist is still baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there is plenty of water there — a detail suggesting baptism by immersion.

f.g: “Springs” — probably in the Jordan Valley.

f.w: because there was much water there

chapters.n: This happened before John was imprisoned by Herod Antipas.
A debate arises between some of John’s disciples and a Jewish man about ritual purification — likely about the meaning of baptism.

f.g: Many manuscripts read “a Jew.”
Ceremonial cleansing rituals.

chapters.n: John’s disciples come to him concerned: the man you testified about is baptizing, and everyone is going to Him! They feel their teacher is being overshadowed.

f.g: An exaggeration showing their worry.

chapters.n: John answers humbly: a person can receive only what heaven gives him. Each has his own God-given role.

f.w: except it be given him from heaven

chapters.n: You yourselves heard me say I am not the Messiah but the one sent ahead of Him.
John uses a wedding image: the bride belongs to the groom. The best man doesn’t envy him — he rejoices to hear the groom’s voice. John’s joy is complete in seeing Christ succeed.

f.g: In scripture, God is pictured as the bridegroom of His people.
Like the best man, who arranged the wedding.

chapters.n: John’s famous words: He must increase, but I must decrease. A model of humility for every servant of Christ.
The one from above is over all. Earthly people speak from an earthly viewpoint; the one from heaven is supreme. Some scholars think verses 31–36 are the Gospel writer’s reflections.
He testifies of what He has personally seen and heard in heaven, yet few accept His testimony.

f.g: A generalization — relatively few, not literally none (see v. 33).

chapters.n: Whoever accepts His testimony puts a seal on it, certifying that God is true. Believing Christ is affirming God’s truthfulness.

f.g: Certified, as with a wax seal on a document.

chapters.n: The one God sent speaks God’s words, for God gives Him the Spirit without limit. The JST adds that the Spirit dwells in Him in fulness.

f.g: Without limit. JST John 3:34 adds: “for he dwelleth in him, even the fulness.”

chapters.n: The Father loves the Son and has entrusted everything into His hands.

f.w: hath given all things into his hand

chapters.n: Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever refuses to obey the Son will not see life, and God’s judgment remains on them. Belief and obedience go together.

f.g: Greek apeitheō — “disobeys,” refuses to obey.
God’s righteous judgment against sin.

chapters.n: Jesus learns that the Pharisees have heard He is gaining and baptizing more disciples than John. Growing attention from the authorities could bring conflict before His time.

f.w: made and baptized more disciples than John

chapters.n: John clarifies that Jesus Himself wasn’t personally baptizing — His disciples did, acting under His authority. The JST says Jesus baptized fewer than His disciples, letting them do it as an example.

f.g: JST John 4:3-4: “he himself baptized not so many as his disciples; for he suffered them for an example, preferring one another.”

chapters.n: So He leaves Judea and heads back north to Galilee.
He “had to” go through Samaria. It was the direct route, but many Jews detoured around it. John hints at a divine necessity — someone there needed Him.

f.g: Had to — perhaps a geographical and a divine necessity.
The central region between Judea and Galilee, home to the Samaritans.

chapters.n: He comes to Sychar, a Samaritan town near land Jacob had given his son Joseph centuries earlier.

f.g: Near ancient Shechem, at the foot of Mount Gerizim.

f.w: the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph

chapters.n: Jacob’s well is there. Tired from walking, Jesus sits by the well around noon — the hottest part of the day. The eternal Word truly shared human weariness.

f.g: A deep well still shown near Nablus today, more than 100 feet deep.
About noon.

chapters.n: A Samaritan woman comes to draw water. Jesus asks her for a drink. Women usually drew water in the cool morning or evening; coming at noon may suggest she was avoiding others.

f.g: By asking a favor, Jesus breaks social barriers and honors her.

chapters.n: His disciples have gone into town to buy food, leaving Jesus alone with her.

f.g: Food.

chapters.n: She is startled: You’re a Jew asking a Samaritan woman for a drink? Jews avoided Samaritans and even their dishes. Jesus crosses ethnic, religious, and gender lines.

f.w: the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans
f.g: Probably “Jews do not share vessels with Samaritans,” for fear of ritual impurity.

chapters.n: Jesus replies: if you knew God’s gift and who is asking you, you would have asked Him, and He would give you “living water.”

f.g: Common phrase for flowing spring water; Jesus uses it for the life He gives.

chapters.n: She takes Him literally: You have no bucket, and the well is deep. Where would you get this living water?

f.g: Travelers carried a leather bucket and rope.

chapters.n: Are You greater than our ancestor Jacob, who gave us this well? Ironically — yes, He is. Samaritans proudly claimed descent from Jacob through Joseph.

f.g: Samaritans claimed descent from the northern tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh.

chapters.n: Jesus points out that anyone who drinks this water will get thirsty again.

f.g: Earthly satisfactions never fully satisfy.

chapters.n: But the water He gives will satisfy forever, becoming a spring inside the person, bubbling up to eternal life. He speaks of the Spirit and the life He gives.

f.w: a well of water springing up into everlasting life

chapters.n: She asks for this water so she won’t be thirsty or have to keep coming to the well. She still thinks physically, but her heart is opening.

f.g: Her request is a step of faith, even if still misunderstood.

chapters.n: Jesus tells her to go call her husband and come back. He is gently opening the painful part of her life.

f.g: Jesus addresses the real need beneath her question.

chapters.n: She says she has no husband. Jesus replies: you’re right to say that.

f.g: You have spoken truly.

chapters.n: He reveals that she has had five husbands, and the man she lives with now isn’t her husband. He knows her completely — yet keeps talking with her, without condemning.

f.g: We are not told why — death, divorce, or both. Women could not easily initiate divorce then.

chapters.n: Astonished, she says: Sir, I can see You are a prophet.

f.g: Her understanding of Jesus keeps rising: a Jew, “Sir,” a prophet, then possibly the Christ.

chapters.n: She raises the great Jewish–Samaritan dispute: our ancestors worshipped on this mountain (Gerizim), but you Jews insist Jerusalem is the place to worship.

f.g: Mount Gerizim, where the Samaritans had a temple until the Jews destroyed it around 110 BC.

chapters.n: Jesus tells her a time is coming when worship of the Father won’t be tied to either place.

f.g: A respectful and earnest appeal.

chapters.n: Samaritans worshipped without fully understanding, accepting only the five books of Moses. Salvation comes through the Jews, for the Messiah descends from them.
The time has now come when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth. The Father seeks such worshippers.

f.g: With sincere hearts and in accordance with revealed truth.

f.w: the Father seeketh such to worship him

chapters.n: The KJV says “God is a Spirit.” The JST reads: “For unto such hath God promised his Spirit,” consistent with the Latter-day Saint teaching that the Father has a glorified body.

f.g: Greek has no “a” — “God is spirit.” JST John 4:26: “For unto such hath God promised his Spirit.”

chapters.n: She says she knows the Messiah is coming, and He will explain everything. Samaritans expected a figure they called the Taheb, “the one who returns” or restores.

f.g: Messiah.

f.w: he will tell us all things

chapters.n: Jesus answers plainly: I who speak to you am He. One of His clearest declarations of His identity is made to a Samaritan woman of questionable reputation.

f.w: I that speak unto thee am he
f.g: Greek egō eimi, “I am” — echoing the divine name.

chapters.n: The disciples return, surprised to find Him talking with a woman — rabbis typically didn’t speak with women in public. But no one dares question Him.

f.g: Were amazed.

chapters.n: The woman leaves her water jar behind — her original errand forgotten — and hurries into town to tell people.

f.g: A small detail showing she has found something more important.

chapters.n: Come see a man who told me everything I ever did! Could this be the Messiah? The woman who avoided people becomes a missionary to them.

f.g: Phrased as a hopeful question — inviting them to judge for themselves.

chapters.n: The townspeople leave the city and come out to Jesus.

f.g: In Greek, “were coming” — a stream of people approaching.

chapters.n: Meanwhile the disciples urge Him to eat.

f.g: Urged, asked Him.

chapters.n: He says He has food they don’t know about.

f.g: Food — here spiritual nourishment.

chapters.n: Puzzled, they ask each other whether someone brought Him food. Like the woman, they think only literally.

f.g: Anything (aught).

chapters.n: His food is doing the will of the One who sent Him and completing His work. Serving God nourishes Him more than bread.

f.w: My meat is to do the will of him that sent me

chapters.n: People say harvest is still four months away, but Jesus says look — the fields are already white for harvest. The Samaritans streaming toward them, perhaps in white clothing, are the harvest.
The reaper already receives wages, gathering a harvest for eternal life, so sower and reaper can rejoice together.
The saying is true: one plants, another harvests.
He sends them to reap what others planted. The prophets, John the Baptist, and now this woman prepared the ground; the disciples gather the fruit.
Many Samaritans in that town believe in Jesus because of the woman’s testimony: He told me everything I ever did.

f.w: believed on him for the saying of the woman
f.g: Her simple testimony was powerful.

chapters.n: They come and urge Him to stay, and He stays two days — a Jew lodging with Samaritans.

f.g: Stay.
Stayed.

chapters.n: Many more believe because of His own words.

f.g: Direct contact with Christ deepens faith begun through others.

chapters.n: They tell the woman: now we believe not just because of what you said, but because we’ve heard Him ourselves. He truly is the Savior of the world — not just of the Jews.

f.g: Testimony must become personal.

chapters.n: After two days, Jesus continues on to Galilee.

f.g: From there.

chapters.n: Jesus Himself had said a prophet isn’t honored in his own homeland — a principle that applies to His reception in Nazareth and Galilee.

f.w: a prophet hath no honour in his own country

chapters.n: The Galileans welcome Him because they had seen what He did at the Passover feast in Jerusalem. Their welcome is based on miracles.
He returns to Cana, where He had turned water to wine. A royal official whose son is ill in Capernaum hears He is there.

f.g: A royal official, probably serving Herod Antipas.

chapters.n: The official travels about twenty miles to find Jesus and begs Him to come heal his son, who is near death.

f.g: Capernaum lies lower, by the lake; Cana is in the hills.
Dying.

chapters.n: Jesus says: unless you people see signs and wonders, you won’t believe. He wants faith that rests on Him, not just on spectacle.
The father doesn’t argue — he just pleads: Sir, come before my child dies.

f.g: Before.

chapters.n: Jesus tells him: Go home; your son lives. The man believes the word alone and leaves. He shows the kind of faith Jesus is seeking — trusting His word without seeing.
On the way home, his servants meet him with the news: your son is alive!

f.g: The servants repeat Jesus’ exact words.

chapters.n: He asks when the boy began to improve. They say: yesterday at the seventh hour, the fever left him.

f.g: About 1 p.m.
Get better.

chapters.n: The father realizes it was the exact moment Jesus spoke. He and his whole household believe — his faith grows from trusting a word to full conversion.

f.g: His entire household — family and servants.

chapters.n: This was the second sign Jesus performed after returning from Judea to Galilee — both at Cana.

f.g: The second of John’s seven signs.

chapters.n: Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for one of the Jewish festivals. John doesn’t name which one; suggestions include Passover, Pentecost, or Tabernacles.

f.g: Unnamed; Jewish men were expected to attend three pilgrimage feasts yearly.

chapters.n: Near the Sheep Gate in Jerusalem is a pool called Bethesda, surrounded by five covered colonnades. Archaeologists have uncovered a large double pool matching this description.

f.g: Better “Sheep Gate,” near the temple’s north side, through which sacrificial sheep entered.
Possibly “house of mercy” or “house of outpouring.”
Roofed colonnades.

chapters.n: Crowds of sick people lie there — blind, lame, and paralyzed — waiting for the water to stir.

f.g: People without strength — invalids.
Lame.
Paralyzed, with shriveled limbs.

chapters.n: This verse explains the popular belief that an angel stirred the water and the first one in was healed. It’s missing from the earliest manuscripts and may have been a later explanatory note. Jesus’ healing doesn’t depend on it.

f.g: Stirred it up — possibly from an intermittent spring feeding the pool.

chapters.n: One man there has been disabled for thirty-eight years — longer than many people lived then.

f.g: Illness or disability.
The same length as Israel’s wandering after Kadesh.

chapters.n: Jesus sees him lying there, knows how long he has suffered, and asks: Do you want to get well? The question invites the man to hope again.

f.g: Do you want to be healed? Jesus engages the man’s will.

chapters.n: The man explains he has no one to help him into the water when it stirs; someone always beats him. After decades, he has no helper and little hope.

f.g: A cry of loneliness as much as a complaint.

chapters.n: Jesus commands: Get up, pick up your mat, and walk. No pool, no angel — just His word.

f.w: Rise, take up thy bed, and walk

f.g: A sleeping mat or pallet.

chapters.n: Instantly the man is healed, picks up his mat, and walks. Then John adds the detail that sets off the conflict: it was the Sabbath.
The religious authorities confront the healed man: it’s the Sabbath; carrying your mat is against the law. They notice the rule, not the miracle.

f.w: not lawful for thee to carry thy bed
f.g: Jewish tradition listed carrying an object from one domain to another among forbidden Sabbath work.

chapters.n: He answers: the man who healed me told me to pick up my mat and walk.

f.g: He defers to the authority of his healer.

chapters.n: They demand to know who told him to do that — more concerned about the rule-breaking than the healing.

f.g: They ask about the command, not the miracle.

chapters.n: The man didn’t know who it was. Jesus had slipped away into the crowd.

f.g: Did not know.
Slipped away quietly.

chapters.n: Later Jesus finds him in the temple: you’ve been healed — stop sinning, or something worse may happen. Spiritual healing matters even more than physical.

f.g: Possibly spiritual or eternal consequences.

chapters.n: The man goes and tells the authorities that Jesus was the one who healed him.

f.g: Whether naive or disloyal, his report brings Jesus under scrutiny.

chapters.n: From then on the leaders begin persecuting Jesus and seeking to kill Him for doing these things on the Sabbath.

f.g: Not in all manuscripts here, but stated plainly in v. 18.

chapters.n: Jesus answers: My Father is working until now, and I am working too. God never stops sustaining creation and doing good, even on the Sabbath — and neither does His Son.

f.g: “Hitherto” means up until now, continually.

chapters.n: This makes them even more determined to kill Him: besides breaking their Sabbath rules, He calls God His own Father, making Himself equal with God.
Jesus explains His relationship with the Father: the Son does nothing on His own but does what He sees the Father doing. Joseph Smith taught this reflects the Son following the Father’s pattern.

f.w: what he seeth the Father do

chapters.n: The Father loves the Son and shows Him everything He does. Even greater works are coming that will amaze them.

f.g: Giving life and judging — the works described next.

chapters.n: Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, the Son gives life to whomever He chooses.

f.g: Makes alive.

chapters.n: The Father has entrusted all judgment to the Son.

f.w: committed all judgment unto the Son

chapters.n: So that all will honor the Son as they honor the Father. Dishonoring the Son is dishonoring the Father who sent Him.

f.w: honour the Son, even as they honour the Father

chapters.n: Whoever hears Jesus’ word and believes the Father who sent Him has eternal life now. They will not be condemned; they have already passed from death to life.

f.w: is passed from death unto life

chapters.n: The time is coming — and is already here — when the dead will hear the voice of God’s Son and live. This is true of the spiritually dead now, and of the dead in the spirit world, to whom Christ would preach.

f.w: the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God

chapters.n: The Father has life in Himself, and He has granted the Son to have life in Himself too. This is why Jesus could lay down His life and take it up again.
The Father has given Him authority to judge because He is the Son of Man — fully sharing our human experience.
Don’t be amazed: the time is coming when all who are in their graves will hear His voice. Resurrection is universal.

f.w: all that are in the graves

chapters.n: They will come out — those who did good to the resurrection of life, those who did evil to the resurrection of judgment. Pondering this verse led Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon to the vision recorded in D&C 76.

f.g: Damnation here means judgment or condemnation. Joseph Smith was directed to render it “resurrection of the unjust.”

chapters.n: Jesus says He does nothing on His own. His judgment is just because He seeks not His own will but the Father’s.

f.w: I seek not mine own will

chapters.n: If He alone testified about Himself, His testimony wouldn’t be legally valid. The law required more than one witness.

f.g: Not legally valid on its own.

chapters.n: But there is another who testifies about Him, and that witness is true — the Father Himself.

f.w: There is another that beareth witness of me

chapters.n: They sent messengers to John the Baptist, and John testified to the truth.
Jesus doesn’t depend on human testimony, but He mentions John’s for their sake, so they might be saved.

f.g: His purpose even in debate is their salvation.

chapters.n: John was like a burning, shining lamp, and for a while they were happy to enjoy his light. But their enthusiasm faded.

f.w: a burning and a shining light
f.g: A lamp — lit by another source, unlike Jesus who is the Light itself.
For a while.

chapters.n: Jesus has a greater witness than John: the works the Father gave Him to accomplish prove the Father sent Him.
The Father Himself has testified of Him. Yet they have never heard His voice or seen His form — because they did not truly know Him.

f.g: His form or appearance.

chapters.n: His word doesn’t live in them, as shown by their refusal to believe the one He sent.

f.g: Remaining, living.

chapters.n: They diligently study the scriptures, thinking that study itself gives eternal life — yet the scriptures point to Jesus.

f.g: In Greek this can be a statement (“You search”) or a command.

f.w: they are they which testify of me

chapters.n: Yet they refuse to come to Him to receive the life the scriptures promise.

f.w: ye will not come to me

chapters.n: Jesus isn’t seeking human praise.

f.g: Glory, approval.

chapters.n: He knows them: they don’t have God’s love in their hearts.

f.g: Either love for God or God’s love — probably both.

chapters.n: He comes in His Father’s name, and they reject Him; yet if someone comes in his own name, they’ll accept him. History saw many false messiahs welcomed.

f.g: With the Father’s authority, as His representative.

chapters.n: How can they believe when they care about each other’s approval but not about the approval that comes from God alone? Seeking praise blocks faith.

f.w: the honour that cometh from God only

chapters.n: Jesus won’t need to accuse them before the Father. Moses, in whom they put their hope, will accuse them.

f.g: They prided themselves on following Moses’ law.

chapters.n: If they truly believed Moses, they would believe Jesus, because Moses wrote about Him.
But if they don’t believe what Moses wrote, how will they believe what Jesus says? Rejecting the earlier witness leads to rejecting the greater one.

f.w: how shall ye believe my words?

chapters.n: Some time later Jesus crosses the Sea of Galilee. John gives its second name, Tiberias, after the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore and named for the Roman emperor.

f.g: Also called the Lake of Gennesaret (Luke 5:1) and Chinnereth in the Old Testament.

chapters.n: Crowds follow him, drawn mostly by the healings they have seen. John quietly sets up the question the chapter will press: why are people following Jesus?

f.g: John’s word is “signs” (Greek sēmeia) — miracles that point beyond themselves to who Jesus is.

chapters.n: Jesus climbs into the hill country above the lake and sits down with his disciples — the posture of a teacher in that culture.
John notes that Passover is near. That detail matters: the feast recalled manna and deliverance from Egypt, and Jesus is about to feed a multitude and call himself the true bread from heaven.
Seeing the huge crowd approaching, Jesus asks Philip where they could buy bread. Philip was from nearby Bethsaida, so the question was natural — but it was also a test.
John explains that Jesus already knew what he would do. He was inviting Philip to stretch his faith beyond what money and markets could supply.

f.g: prove = test, try out. The aim was to strengthen Philip, not trap him.

chapters.n: Philip does the math: even two hundred days’ wages would not buy enough for each person to get a bite. Human resources are plainly not enough.

f.g: Two hundred denarii. A denarius was roughly one day’s pay for a laborer, so this is about eight months’ wages.

chapters.n: Andrew, who earlier brought his brother Peter to Jesus, steps forward with what little he has found.
A boy has five barley loaves and two small fish. Barley bread was the cheap food of the poor. Andrew offers it while admitting it seems useless — yet Jesus uses small offerings.

f.g: Elisha also fed a crowd with barley loaves, and there was food left over.
Probably dried or salted fish eaten with bread, common around the lake.

chapters.n: Jesus has the people sit on the spring grass. About five thousand men are counted, besides women and children, which makes this the only miracle besides the Resurrection found in all four Gospels.

f.g: Green grass fits the spring Passover season noted in verse 4.

chapters.n: Jesus gives thanks and the food is shared until everyone has as much as they want. The actions — taking, giving thanks, distributing — echo the Last Supper and the sacrament.
Jesus tells the disciples to gather the leftovers so nothing is wasted. God’s abundance is generous, but never careless.
Twelve baskets of leftovers are collected — far more than the five loaves they began with. Some see the number twelve as a hint that Jesus can feed all the tribes of Israel.

f.g: Greek kophinos — a sturdy wicker basket travelers carried.

chapters.n: The crowd concludes Jesus must be “that prophet” Moses promised — a new Moses who, like the first, provides bread in the wilderness.

f.w: that prophet that should come into the world

chapters.n: Realizing they intend to force him to be their king, Jesus slips away alone into the hills. He would not become the political, bread-giving deliverer they wanted.

f.g: Matthew and Mark add that he went up to pray.

chapters.n: As evening falls the disciples go down to the shore without him.

f.g: even = evening.

chapters.n: They set out by boat across the lake toward Capernaum. It is now dark and Jesus has not joined them — a scene of being alone and in the dark.

f.g: A fishing town on the north shore that served as Jesus’s home base in Galilee.

chapters.n: A strong wind stirs up the water. The Sea of Galilee sits low among hills, and sudden storms still sweep down on it.
After rowing about three or four miles, they see Jesus walking on the water toward them and are terrified.

f.w: five and twenty or thirty furlongs
f.g: A furlong (Greek stadion) was about 600 feet, so 25–30 furlongs is roughly 3 to 3½ miles.

chapters.n: Jesus calms them: “It is I; don’t be afraid.” In Greek his words are literally “I am” — an echo of the divine name that John will develop throughout this Gospel.

f.g: Greek egō eimi, “I am.”

chapters.n: Gladly they take him aboard, and right away the boat reaches shore. John lets the abrupt arrival hint at more power at work.

f.w: immediately the ship was at the land

chapters.n: The next day the crowd on the far shore puzzle over Jesus: there had been only one boat, and he had not gotten into it with the disciples.

f.g: John includes these details to show the crowd could not explain how Jesus had crossed.

chapters.n: In a side note, John explains that other boats had come over from Tiberias, near the place of the feeding — which is how the crowd could follow.

f.w: after that the Lord had given thanks
f.g: John again highlights the thanksgiving, as if it were the heart of the meal.

chapters.n: Unable to find Jesus or his disciples, the people board boats and sail to Capernaum to look for him.

f.g: Seeking Jesus is good — but the next verses ask why they are seeking him.

chapters.n: Finding him, they call him “Rabbi” and ask when he arrived. They want an explanation of the crossing; Jesus will answer a deeper question instead.

f.g: Rabbi = “my teacher,” a respectful title.

chapters.n: Jesus gently exposes their motive: they came back not because the miracle pointed them to God but because they got a free meal.

f.g: Greek amēn, amēn — “truly, truly.” John alone records Jesus doubling it for solemn emphasis.

chapters.n: Don’t spend your life working for food that spoils, Jesus says; seek the food that lasts forever, which he will give. The Father has put his seal of approval on him.

f.g: meat = food in general, not only flesh.
Like a seal stamped on a document — the Father has authenticated and authorized his Son.

chapters.n: Picking up his word “labour,” the crowd ask what works they must do to please God, expecting a list of duties.
Jesus answers that the essential “work” God asks is to believe in the One he has sent. Real faith in Christ is where all righteous works begin.

f.w: believe on him whom he hath sent

chapters.n: Astonishingly, the same people who were fed the day before ask for a sign to prove Jesus’s claim.

f.g: shewest = showest.

chapters.n: They hint at the sign they want: Moses gave their ancestors manna every day for forty years, so surely the Messiah should match that.
Jesus corrects them on two points: it was God, not Moses, who gave the manna; and the Father is now giving the true, lasting bread from heaven.
God’s bread is not a substance but a person — the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the whole world.
Like the Samaritan woman asking for living water, they ask for this bread always — still thinking of something physical.
Jesus makes the first of his great “I am” statements in John: he himself is the bread of life. Coming to him and believing in him satisfies the soul’s deepest hunger and thirst.

f.w: I am the bread of life

chapters.n: Jesus reminds them that they have seen him with their own eyes and still refuse to believe. Seeing miracles alone does not produce faith.

f.w: have seen me, and believe not

chapters.n: Everyone the Father gives to Jesus will come to him, and Jesus will never turn away anyone who comes. This is one of the most reassuring promises in scripture.

f.w: I will in no wise cast out

chapters.n: Jesus describes his entire mission as doing his Father’s will rather than his own — the same submission he will show in Gethsemane.

f.w: not to do mine own will

chapters.n: The Father’s will is that Jesus lose none of those entrusted to him and raise them up at the last day. Christ’s care for us reaches all the way to the Resurrection.

f.g: The day of resurrection and judgment at the end of the world.

chapters.n: Anyone who truly sees the Son for who he is and believes in him will have eternal life, and Jesus will raise them in the Resurrection.
The listeners grumble, much as Israel grumbled against Moses over food in the wilderness.

f.g: murmur = grumble or complain under the breath.

chapters.n: They object that they know his family: how can the son of Joseph, a local man, claim to have come down from heaven? Familiarity blinds them.
Jesus tells them to stop grumbling among themselves.

f.g: A gentle rebuke — complaining shuts out the very teaching that could help them.

chapters.n: No one comes to Christ unless the Father draws them. God takes the first step, reaching for every heart; those who respond will be raised up at the last day.

f.w: except the Father which hath sent me draw him
f.g: The JST stresses that a person comes to Christ by doing the will of the Father and receiving the Son.

chapters.n: Jesus quotes Isaiah: in the messianic age all will be taught by God. Anyone who truly listens to the Father will recognize the Son and come to him.

f.w: they shall be all taught of God

chapters.n: Being taught by the Father doesn’t mean everyone has seen him. Only the one who comes from God — Jesus — has truly seen the Father and can reveal him.

f.g: The JST of John 1:18 adds that no one has seen God “except he hath borne record of the Son.”

chapters.n: With a solemn “truly, truly,” Jesus states plainly: whoever believes in him has eternal life — present tense. It begins now.
Jesus repeats the heart of his message in five words.

f.w: I am that bread of life

chapters.n: The manna kept their ancestors alive for a time, but those people still died. Even miraculous earthly bread cannot conquer death.
By contrast, the bread from heaven Jesus offers is meant to be eaten so a person never dies spiritually.
Jesus now calls himself the “living bread” and makes the meaning explicit: the bread is his flesh, which he will give up in death so the world can live. Here the sermon turns toward his Atonement.

f.w: my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world

chapters.n: The audience argues sharply among themselves, taking his words literally: how could anyone eat his flesh?

f.g: strove = argued heatedly, quarreled.

chapters.n: Rather than softening his words, Jesus intensifies them: unless we eat his flesh and drink his blood we have no life in us. He means taking his atoning sacrifice fully into our lives.

f.g: Jewish law forbade drinking blood (Leviticus 17:10-14), which made this saying deeply shocking.

chapters.n: Whoever feeds on Christ in this way — by faith, covenant, and continual dependence on him — has eternal life and will be raised at the last day.

f.g: The Greek verb here (trōgō) is vivid — “to chew” — stressing real, personal partaking.

chapters.n: His flesh is real food and his blood real drink: only Christ truly nourishes the spirit.

f.g: indeed = truly, genuinely.

chapters.n: Partaking of Christ creates a living union: he dwells in us and we in him. The sacrament renews that relationship each week.

f.w: dwelleth in me, and I in him

chapters.n: Just as Jesus draws his life from the living Father, those who “feed” on Jesus draw their life from him. Life flows from the Father, through the Son, to us.
Jesus sums up: he is the bread from heaven, unlike manna that could not prevent death. Whoever feeds on him will live forever.
John notes the setting: this sermon was given in the synagogue at Capernaum, where the remains of a later stone synagogue can still be seen today.

f.g: A synagogue was a local Jewish meeting house for prayer and reading the scriptures.

chapters.n: Many of his own followers find the teaching too hard to accept. Here “hard” means offensive or unacceptable, not merely difficult to understand.

f.g: Greek sklēros — harsh, hard to stomach.

chapters.n: Knowing their grumbling, Jesus asks whether this teaching makes them stumble.

f.g: offend = cause to stumble or fall away (Greek skandalizō).

chapters.n: If his coming down from heaven offends them, what will they think when they see him go back up to where he was before? Jesus points ahead to his ascension.

f.w: ascend up where he was before

chapters.n: Jesus clarifies that he is not speaking of physically eating flesh. It is the Spirit that gives life; his words are spirit and life to those who receive them.

f.g: quicken = make alive.

f.w: they are spirit, and they are life

chapters.n: Still, some of them do not believe. John adds that Jesus knew from the beginning who would not believe and who would betray him.
This is why, Jesus says, no one can come to him unless it is granted by the Father — coming to Christ is both an invitation from God and a choice we make.

f.w: given unto him of my Father

chapters.n: A sad turning point: many disciples stop following him. Popularity based on bread could not survive a call to deeper discipleship.
Jesus turns to the Twelve and asks, perhaps with sorrow, if they want to leave too. He never forces anyone to stay.

f.g: In Greek the question is phrased in a way that expects “no” for an answer.

chapters.n: Peter answers for the Twelve with one of scripture’s great testimonies: there is nowhere else to go, because only Jesus has the words that lead to eternal life.
Peter adds that they believe and know Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. Many manuscripts read “the Holy One of God.”

f.g: Faith first, then sure knowledge — the order Alma describes.

chapters.n: Jesus replies that he chose all twelve of them, yet one is “a devil” — an adversary working against him.

f.g: Greek diabolos — slanderer or adversary. Judas would side with Satan’s purposes.

chapters.n: John identifies the one Jesus meant: Judas Iscariot, son of Simon, one of the very Twelve, who would later betray him.

f.g: “Iscariot” may mean “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea.

chapters.n: Jesus stays in Galilee for a while because the leaders in Judea are now plotting to kill him. In John, “the Jews” usually means the hostile religious authorities, not the Jewish people as a whole.

f.g: Jewry = Judea, the southern region around Jerusalem.

chapters.n: The autumn Feast of Tabernacles is approaching — a joyful week-long festival when families lived in leafy booths to remember Israel’s wilderness journey.

f.g: Also called Sukkot or the Feast of Booths; one of three pilgrimage feasts to Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Jesus’s brothers urge him to go to Judea and show his miracles where they will be noticed, so his followers there can see them.

f.g: Younger brothers in Mary’s family: James, Joses, Simon, and Judas.

chapters.n: Their reasoning sounds practical — nobody who wants fame works in secret — but it reveals they see his mission as a bid for public popularity.

f.g: shew = show. Compare Satan’s similar challenge to display power in Matthew 4:5-6.

chapters.n: John explains that even Jesus’s own brothers did not yet believe in him. Later, after the Resurrection, they would become believers and leaders.

f.w: neither did his brethren believe in him

chapters.n: Jesus answers that his timing is set by his Father’s plan; theirs is not, so any time suits them.

f.w: My time is not yet come

f.g: alway = always.

chapters.n: The world has no reason to hate them, since they fit in; it hates Jesus because he exposes its evil deeds.
He tells them to go on to the feast without him; he isn’t going up yet, because his appointed time hasn’t fully arrived.

f.g: Many manuscripts read “I go not up,” but the sense is that he would not go publicly with them on their terms.

chapters.n: So Jesus remains in Galilee for the moment.

f.g: abode = stayed, remained.

chapters.n: After his brothers leave, Jesus goes up quietly, without a public procession. He goes on God’s timetable, not as a show.

f.g: Privately, avoiding the crowds of pilgrims on the road.

chapters.n: At the festival the authorities are looking for him and keep asking where he is.

f.g: Their question shows he is already the talk of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: The crowds whisper and argue: some call him a good man, others a deceiver leading people astray.

f.g: Here, low-voiced debate and gossip among the crowds.

chapters.n: Yet no one dares speak openly about him because they fear the religious leaders.
Halfway through the week-long feast, Jesus appears in the temple courts and begins teaching publicly.

f.g: About the fourth day of the eight-day festival.

chapters.n: The leaders are amazed that he knows the scriptures so well without having studied under a recognized rabbi.

f.g: letters = learning, especially formal training in the scriptures.

chapters.n: Jesus explains that his teaching isn’t his own invention; it comes from the Father who sent him. His authority is divine, not academic.
Here is a key promise: anyone willing to live God’s will can come to know for themselves whether Jesus’s teaching is from God. Obedience opens the door to testimony.

f.w: If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine

chapters.n: A self-promoter seeks his own glory; one who seeks to glorify the one who sent him can be trusted. Jesus points glory to the Father.
Jesus turns the tables: Moses gave them the law, yet they don’t keep it — and plotting murder breaks it outright.

f.w: Why go ye about to kill me?

chapters.n: The crowd, unaware of their leaders’ plot, accuse him of being possessed or paranoid.

f.g: An insult meaning “you’re crazy” or “a demon is speaking through you.”

chapters.n: Jesus refers to the one miracle that caused so much uproar on his last visit — healing the paralyzed man at Bethesda on the Sabbath.
He points out that they circumcise baby boys even on the Sabbath when the eighth day falls then — a practice that goes back to the patriarchs, before Moses.

f.g: From Abraham and the patriarchs, long before the law of Moses.

chapters.n: If they will perform a ritual on one part of the body on the Sabbath to keep the law, why be angry at him for making a whole person well on the Sabbath?

f.g: every whit = completely, in every part.

chapters.n: Stop judging by surface appearances, he urges; judge fairly and righteously.
Some Jerusalem residents, who know about the plot, wonder aloud whether this is the man the leaders want to kill.

f.g: Local residents, as opposed to the pilgrims visiting for the feast.

chapters.n: They are puzzled that he speaks boldly and no one stops him. Could the rulers have secretly concluded he is the Messiah?

f.g: Christ = Greek for “Anointed One,” the same meaning as the Hebrew “Messiah.”

chapters.n: They dismiss the idea: they know where he’s from, while popular belief held that the Messiah would appear from an unknown origin.

f.w: no man knoweth whence he is
f.g: A popular belief that the Messiah would be hidden until suddenly revealed.

chapters.n: Jesus calls out in the temple: they know his earthly hometown, but not his true origin. He has been sent by the Father — whom they do not truly know.
Jesus, by contrast, knows the Father personally because he comes from him and was sent by him.
They try to arrest him, but no one can lay a hand on him, because his “hour” — the time of his suffering and death — has not yet come.

f.w: his hour was not yet come

chapters.n: Meanwhile many ordinary people believe, reasoning that the Messiah could hardly do more miracles than this man.

f.w: many of the people believed on him

chapters.n: Hearing this support grow, the Pharisees and chief priests send temple police to arrest him.

f.g: Temple guards under the authority of the chief priests.
The high priest and leading members of the priestly families, mostly Sadducees.

chapters.n: Jesus says he will be with them only a little longer before returning to the Father who sent him.

f.w: Yet a little while am I with you

chapters.n: They will look for him and not find him, because they cannot follow where he is going — into the presence of God.

f.w: where I am, thither ye cannot come
f.g: thither = there, to that place.

chapters.n: His hearers misunderstand, guessing he will go teach Jews scattered abroad or even Gentiles. Ironically, his gospel would soon go to the Gentiles.

f.g: The Diaspora — Jews living outside the land of Israel.

chapters.n: They puzzle over his words but don’t grasp them.

f.w: What manner of saying is this
f.g: What kind of statement is this?

chapters.n: On the final, greatest day of the feast — when priests poured water at the altar praying for rain — Jesus stands and cries out: anyone who is thirsty should come to him and drink.

f.w: If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink
f.g: During the feast a priest drew water from the Pool of Siloam and poured it at the altar each morning.

chapters.n: Whoever believes in him will become a source of “living water” — life flowing out to others, as the prophets foresaw.

f.g: belly = the innermost being, the heart.

chapters.n: John explains that the living water is the Holy Ghost, whom believers would receive after Jesus was glorified through his death and resurrection.

f.w: the Holy Ghost was not yet given
f.g: The JST reads that the Holy Ghost “was promised unto them who believe, after that Jesus was glorified.”

chapters.n: Some listeners now conclude that Jesus is “the Prophet” whom Moses foretold.
Others declare he is the Messiah. But skeptics object that the Messiah could not come from Galilee.

f.w: Shall Christ come out of Galilee?

chapters.n: They cite scripture: the Messiah is to be David’s descendant from Bethlehem. Ironically, Jesus was both — they simply didn’t know his story.
The crowd splits into factions over him. Jesus often divides people because he requires a decision.
Some want to seize him, yet no one actually does.

f.w: no man laid hands on him

chapters.n: The temple officers return empty-handed, and the leaders demand to know why.

f.w: Why have ye not brought him?

chapters.n: The officers’ answer is a remarkable testimony from unlikely witnesses: no one has ever spoken the way this man speaks.

f.w: Never man spake like this man

chapters.n: The Pharisees sneer: have the officers been fooled too?

f.g: led astray.

chapters.n: They argue from authority: none of the rulers or Pharisees believe — as if truth depended on the approval of the elite.

f.g: Members of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: They dismiss the common people as ignorant of the law and therefore cursed — a contemptuous attitude Jesus repeatedly rejected.

f.w: this people who knoweth not the law

chapters.n: Nicodemus, himself a member of the council who once came to Jesus by night, speaks up.
He reminds them that their own law forbids condemning a person without first hearing him and learning the facts. Quietly, Nicodemus is beginning to stand for Jesus.

f.w: Doth our law judge any man, before it hear him

chapters.n: They mock him as a Galilean sympathizer and claim no prophet comes from Galilee — overlooking that Jonah was from Gath-hepher in Galilee.

f.w: out of Galilee ariseth no prophet

chapters.n: The meeting breaks up and everyone goes home, the question about Jesus still unresolved.

f.w: every man went unto his own house
f.g: Many ancient manuscripts lack the passage from here through John 8:11, though it is widely regarded as a genuine story about Jesus.

chapters.n: While others go home, Jesus goes out to the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley, where he often spent the night during visits to the city.
At dawn he is back in the temple courts. People gather, and he sits down to teach them, as rabbis did.

f.w: he sat down, and taught them

chapters.n: Religious leaders interrupt, dragging in a woman caught in adultery and making her stand in front of everyone — a public humiliation.

f.g: Experts who copied, studied, and interpreted the law of Moses.

chapters.n: They address Jesus as “Master” (teacher) and stress she was caught in the act. Pointedly, the man involved is nowhere to be seen.

f.g: The law required that both the man and the woman be punished.

chapters.n: They cite the law of Moses that such people be stoned and demand Jesus’s ruling.
It is a trap: if he says to spare her, he contradicts Moses; if he says to stone her, he loses his reputation for mercy and defies Roman rule. Jesus quietly stoops and writes in the dust.

f.g: tempting = testing, trying to trap.
John doesn’t say what he wrote; many have guessed, but the text leaves it unknown.

chapters.n: When they keep pressing, Jesus stands and says: let the one without sin throw the first stone. He upholds the law while turning their judgment back on their own hearts.

f.w: He that is without sin among you
f.g: Under the law, the witnesses were to throw the first stones.

chapters.n: Then he bends down and writes on the ground again, giving them time to think.

f.g: Some see an echo of Jeremiah: those who forsake the Lord “shall be written in the earth.”

chapters.n: Their consciences pierced, the accusers slip away one by one, oldest first, until only Jesus and the woman are left.

f.g: Perhaps the older men, with more life experience, recognized their own sins first.

chapters.n: Jesus stands and speaks to her gently, calling her “Woman” — a respectful form of address — and asks where her accusers have gone.

f.g: A polite term in that culture, not cold or rude.

chapters.n: She answers that no one has condemned her. Jesus, the only sinless one present, does not condemn her either — but he calls her to leave her sin behind. Mercy and the call to change come together.

f.w: Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more
f.g: The JST adds: “And the woman glorified God from that hour, and believed on his name.”

chapters.n: Jesus declares, “I am the light of the world.” During this feast huge lamps were lit in the temple court; Jesus claims to be the true light that guides people out of darkness.

f.w: I am the light of the world

chapters.n: The Pharisees object that a man’s testimony about himself proves nothing legally.
Jesus replies that his testimony is still valid because he knows where he came from and where he is going — something they don’t know.

f.w: whence I came, and whither I go
f.g: whence = from where; whither = to where.

chapters.n: They judge by outward, human standards; Jesus did not come at this time to condemn anyone.

f.g: By merely human, worldly standards.

chapters.n: And when he does judge, his judgment is true, because he doesn’t judge alone — the Father who sent him is with him.
He points to their own law, which requires two witnesses to establish a matter.

f.w: the testimony of two men is true

chapters.n: He meets that standard: he is one witness, and his Father is the second. The Father and the Son are separate witnesses in perfect agreement.

f.w: the Father that sent me beareth witness of me

chapters.n: They ask where his Father is, thinking of an earthly father. Jesus answers that they know neither him nor the Father; to know Jesus is to know the Father.

f.w: ye should have known my Father also

chapters.n: John notes the location — the treasury area of the temple, near the offering chests in the Court of the Women. Still no one arrests him, because his hour hasn’t come.

f.g: Thirteen trumpet-shaped offering chests stood in the Court of the Women.

f.w: his hour was not yet come

chapters.n: Jesus warns again that he is going away. Those who reject him will die still burdened by their sins and cannot follow him to God.
His enemies mockingly wonder if he plans to kill himself, misreading his words about going where they can’t come.

f.g: A cruel joke; John’s readers know he will lay down his life, not take it (John 10:18).

chapters.n: Jesus contrasts their origin with his: they belong to this fallen world; he comes from above, from heaven.
That’s why they will die in their sins unless they believe that “I am he.” In Greek Jesus simply says “I am,” echoing God’s name revealed to Moses.

f.g: The word “he” is supplied by the translators; Jesus says egō eimi, “I am.”

chapters.n: “Who are you?” they demand. Jesus replies that he is exactly who he has told them from the start.
He could say much in judgment of them, but he speaks only what he has heard from his truthful Father.

f.w: those things which I have heard of him

chapters.n: John notes that they still didn’t realize he was talking about God the Father.
When they “lift up” the Son of Man — on the cross — they will recognize that he is the “I am,” acting only as the Father taught him.

f.w: lifted up the Son of man

chapters.n: The Father has not left him alone, because Jesus always does what pleases him. Perfect obedience means constant companionship with God.

f.w: I do always those things that please him

chapters.n: Even amid the conflict, many people put their faith in him as he speaks.
To these new believers Jesus explains true discipleship: it means continuing — staying, living — in his word, not just a moment of enthusiasm.

f.w: If ye continue in my word

chapters.n: They will come to know the truth, and that truth will set them free — from sin, error, and fear.

f.w: the truth shall make you free

chapters.n: Offended, some answer that as Abraham’s descendants they have never been slaves to anyone — a bold claim given Egypt, Babylon, and the Roman occupation.
Jesus explains the bondage he means: anyone who commits sin becomes its slave.

f.g: servant = slave (Greek doulos).

chapters.n: A slave has no permanent place in a household, but a son belongs there forever.
So if the Son sets them free, they will be truly free. Real freedom comes through Christ.
Yes, they are Abraham’s physical descendants — but they want to kill him because his word has found no room in their hearts.

f.w: my word hath no place in you

chapters.n: Jesus speaks what he has seen with his Father; they act on what they have learned from their “father” — a hint he will make plain in verse 44.

f.g: Jesus is speaking of spiritual parentage — whose example they follow.

chapters.n: They insist Abraham is their father. Jesus replies that true children of Abraham would act like Abraham — in faith and obedience.
Abraham welcomed God’s messengers; he never tried to kill someone who spoke God’s truth.
They retort that they are not illegitimate — perhaps a sly jab at the rumors about Jesus’s birth — and claim God alone as their Father.

f.w: We be not born of fornication
f.g: Possibly an insult implying doubts about Jesus’s own birth.

chapters.n: If God were truly their Father, they would love Jesus, because he came from God and was sent by him.

f.w: I proceeded forth and came from God

chapters.n: They can’t understand his words because they are unwilling to really hear them.
In his strongest rebuke, Jesus says their true father is the devil, whose desires they carry out. Satan has been a murderer and a liar from the beginning.
Because Jesus tells them the truth, they refuse to believe him — the opposite of what should happen.
Jesus challenges anyone to prove him guilty of a single sin. No one can. So why not believe the truth he speaks?

f.w: Which of you convinceth me of sin?
f.g: convinceth = convicts, proves guilty.

chapters.n: Those who belong to God listen to God’s words. Their refusal to listen shows where they really stand.

f.w: He that is of God heareth God's words

chapters.n: They hurl insults: he is a Samaritan — a despised outsider — and possessed by a demon.

f.g: Jews and Samaritans had centuries of hostility over religion and ancestry.

chapters.n: Jesus calmly denies the charge. He honors his Father, while they dishonor him.
He isn’t seeking glory for himself; God the Father seeks his honor and will be the judge.

f.w: I seek not mine own glory

chapters.n: Then a great promise: anyone who keeps his word will never experience death — meaning spiritual death, separation from God.
His opponents take it literally: Abraham and the prophets died, so how can Jesus promise no one will taste death?

f.g: An idiom for experiencing death.

chapters.n: “Are you greater than Abraham?” they ask. Who does he think he is? The answer, as John’s readers know, is yes.
Jesus replies that self-praise would be worthless; it is his Father — the God they claim — who honors him.

f.w: it is my Father that honoureth me

chapters.n: They don’t really know God, but he does. To deny that would make him a liar; he knows the Father and keeps his word.

f.w: I know him, and keep his saying

chapters.n: Jesus says Abraham rejoiced to see his day — he saw it and was glad. Latter-day scripture confirms that Abraham and other ancient prophets saw and knew of Christ.

f.w: Abraham rejoiced to see my day

chapters.n: They scoff: he isn’t even fifty years old, yet claims to have seen Abraham, who lived some two thousand years before?

f.g: A round number meaning “you’re still a young man”; Jesus was probably in his early thirties.

chapters.n: Jesus makes his boldest claim: before Abraham was born, “I am.” He identifies himself as the eternal God who spoke to Moses — Jehovah, the premortal Christ.

f.g: Latter-day Saints understand Jesus Christ to be Jehovah, the God of the Old Testament.

chapters.n: Understanding the claim, they grab stones to execute him for blasphemy. But Jesus slips away through the crowd and leaves the temple — his hour still had not come.

f.w: going through the midst of them

chapters.n: Walking through Jerusalem, Jesus notices a man who has been blind since birth. Jesus sees him first — the man doesn’t ask for help.

f.g: John stresses this detail; healing congenital blindness was unheard of (see verse 32).

chapters.n: The disciples voice a common belief that suffering is punishment for sin, and wonder whose sin caused this — his own, or his parents’?

f.w: who did sin, this man, or his parents

chapters.n: Jesus rejects the blame game. This blindness isn’t punishment; it is an opportunity for God’s work to be displayed in the man’s life.

f.w: that the works of God should be made manifest in him
f.g: manifest = shown openly.

chapters.n: Jesus feels urgency: he must do his Father’s work while the daylight of his mortal ministry lasts, for the night of his death is coming.

f.w: the night cometh, when no man can work

chapters.n: While he is in the world, he is its light — and he is about to demonstrate it by giving sight to a blind man.

f.w: I am the light of the world

chapters.n: Jesus spits on the ground, makes mud, and spreads it on the man’s eyes. Some see a link to God forming man from the dust; the act also gave a blind man something to feel and do.

f.g: anointed = smeared, applied.

chapters.n: Jesus sends him to wash in the Pool of Siloam, whose name means “Sent.” The man obeys in faith, washes, and comes back able to see.

f.g: A pool at the south end of Jerusalem fed by Hezekiah’s tunnel; its remains have been excavated.
Jesus himself is repeatedly called the one “sent” by the Father in John.

chapters.n: His neighbors and those who knew him as a beggar are stunned and ask whether this is really the same man.

f.g: With few other options, blind people often begged near the temple or city gates.

chapters.n: Some say yes, others think it must be a look-alike; the man himself insists, “I am he.”

f.g: He uses the same Greek phrase, egō eimi, that Jesus uses of himself, though here simply meaning “It’s me.”

chapters.n: So they ask him how his eyes were opened.

f.g: This question is asked repeatedly in the chapter (verses 15, 19, 26).

chapters.n: He tells the simple facts: “a man called Jesus” made mud, told him to wash, and now he sees. At this point he knows little about Jesus — watch his understanding grow.

f.w: A man that is called Jesus
f.g: His view of Jesus grows: a man (v. 11), a prophet (v. 17), from God (v. 33), Lord to be worshipped (v. 38).

chapters.n: Asked where Jesus is, he admits he doesn’t know.

f.g: He had never seen Jesus — he was still blind when Jesus sent him away.

chapters.n: The neighbors bring the formerly blind man to the Pharisees, the religious experts.

f.g: aforetime = previously.

chapters.n: John adds the crucial detail: it was the Sabbath. Kneading clay and healing a non-life-threatening condition broke the rabbis’ Sabbath rules.
The Pharisees question him, and he briefly repeats what happened.

f.g: His account gets shorter as the questioning goes on.

chapters.n: The Pharisees split: some say Jesus can’t be from God since he broke the Sabbath; others ask how a sinner could do such miracles.
They ask the man’s opinion, and he declares boldly that Jesus is a prophet.
The leaders refuse to believe the man was ever blind until they summon his parents.

f.g: Unbelief here is a choice not to accept the evidence.

chapters.n: They ask the parents three things: is this your son, was he born blind, and how does he now see?

f.w: how then doth he now see?
f.g: doth = does.

chapters.n: The parents confirm he is their son and was born blind.

f.g: They will testify only to what is safe.

chapters.n: But they carefully avoid saying how he was healed or by whom, telling the leaders to ask their adult son himself.

f.g: He is an adult, legally able to testify for himself (thirteen or older under Jewish custom).

chapters.n: John explains: the parents were afraid, because the leaders had decided that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Messiah would be expelled from the synagogue.

f.g: Expulsion meant being cut off from community worship and social life.

chapters.n: That fear is why they pass the question back to their son.

f.g: Their caution contrasts with their son’s growing courage.

chapters.n: Recalling the man, the leaders order him to “give God the praise” — an oath formula meaning “tell the truth before God” — and declare that Jesus is a sinner.

f.g: A solemn charge to confess the truth, as Joshua said to Achan.

chapters.n: His answer is one of the great testimonies in scripture: he can’t settle theological debates, but he knows one thing — he was blind, and now he sees.

f.w: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see

chapters.n: They ask again how Jesus opened his eyes, hoping to catch a contradiction.

f.g: They are looking for evidence of Sabbath-breaking.

chapters.n: Exasperated, he says he already told them. Then, with sharp irony, he asks whether they want to become Jesus’s disciples too.

f.w: will ye also be his disciples?
f.g: The word “also” hints he already thinks of himself as a disciple.

chapters.n: They heap insults on him: he can be Jesus’s disciple, but they are disciples of Moses.

f.g: reviled = abused with insulting words.

chapters.n: They know God spoke to Moses, they say, but they don’t know where this fellow comes from.
The man marvels: the experts can’t tell where Jesus comes from, yet Jesus opened his eyes. Isn’t the answer obvious?

f.g: An amazing thing — he is gently mocking their blindness.

chapters.n: He reasons from common belief: God doesn’t answer the prayers of the wicked, but listens to those who worship him and do his will.
Never in history has anyone given sight to a person born blind. Something divine has happened.
His conclusion: if Jesus weren’t from God, he could do nothing at all.

f.w: If this man were not of God
