chapters.n: Unable to answer, they insult him as someone born steeped in sin and throw him out. The man has lost his community for telling the truth.

f.g: Probably expelled from the synagogue, as threatened in verse 22.

chapters.n: Jesus hears about it and seeks the man out. The Good Shepherd finds the one who was cast out and asks if he believes in the Son of God.

f.g: Many early manuscripts read “Son of man.”

chapters.n: He is eager: tell me who he is, Lord, so I can believe in him.

f.g: Here probably “Sir,” though the word deepens in meaning by verse 38.

chapters.n: Jesus reveals himself: you have seen him — the very one now speaking with you. For a man born blind, “you have seen him” carries special joy.

f.w: it is he that talketh with thee

chapters.n: The man believes and worships Jesus. His journey from physical sight to spiritual sight is complete.
Jesus explains the result of his coming: those who know they are blind receive sight, while those who think they see are shown to be blind.

f.w: that they which see not might see

chapters.n: Some Pharisees nearby bristle: surely he doesn’t mean they are blind?
If they admitted their blindness, they could be healed. But claiming to see while rejecting the light leaves their sin in place. Pride blocks the cure.

f.w: If ye were blind, ye should have no sin

chapters.n: Still speaking to the Pharisees who had cast out the healed man, Jesus begins a parable: anyone who sneaks into the sheepfold some other way than the gate is a thief.

f.g: A walled pen, often of stones with thorns on top, where flocks were kept at night.

chapters.n: The true shepherd comes openly through the door. He has every right to be there.
The gatekeeper lets him in, the sheep recognize his voice, and he calls each one by name and leads them out. Christ knows his followers personally.

f.g: porter = gatekeeper or doorkeeper.

f.w: he calleth his own sheep by name

chapters.n: Eastern shepherds walked ahead of their flocks rather than driving them from behind. The sheep follow because they know his voice.
Sheep will run from a stranger’s voice. Disciples learn to tell Christ’s voice from voices that would lead them astray.

f.w: they know not the voice of strangers

chapters.n: The listeners don’t grasp his meaning, so he explains further.

f.g: John uses a word (paroimia) meaning a figure of speech or extended image.

chapters.n: Jesus identifies himself as the door — the only legitimate way into God’s fold.

f.w: I am the door of the sheep
f.g: Some shepherds slept across the opening of the fold, literally becoming the door.

chapters.n: Those who came before claiming to lead God’s people for their own gain were thieves, and the true sheep did not listen to them.

f.w: All that ever came before me
f.g: The JST reads “All that ever came before me who testified not of me are thieves and robbers” — not the true prophets.

chapters.n: Entering through Christ brings salvation, safety, freedom to come and go, and nourishing pasture.
The thief only steals, kills, and destroys. Jesus came to give life — and life in overflowing abundance.
“I am the good shepherd,” Jesus says, and the mark of a good shepherd is that he gives his life for the sheep — a clear foreshadowing of the cross.

f.w: giveth his life for the sheep

chapters.n: A hired hand who doesn’t own the sheep runs at the first sight of a wolf, leaving the flock to be attacked and scattered.

f.g: A hired worker paid for the job, with no personal stake in the sheep.

chapters.n: He runs because he’s only working for wages and doesn’t truly care about the sheep.
Jesus repeats that he is the good shepherd, and adds a mutual, personal relationship: he knows his sheep and they know him.

f.w: know my sheep, and am known of mine

chapters.n: That relationship mirrors the one between the Father and the Son — deep and personal — and it is why he lays down his life for them.
He has other sheep not of this fold whom he must also gather. The Book of Mormon records that Jesus identified the Nephites as these other sheep and visited them after his resurrection.

f.w: other sheep I have, which are not of this fold

chapters.n: The Father loves him because he willingly lays down his life — in order to take it up again in the Resurrection.

f.w: that I might take it again

chapters.n: No one can take his life by force; he gives it voluntarily, with power both to die and to rise again — a power he possessed as the Son of a mortal mother and an immortal Father.

f.w: I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again

chapters.n: Once again the listeners are divided over his words.
Many say he is demon-possessed and insane, and wonder why anyone listens to him.

f.g: mad = insane, out of his mind.

chapters.n: Others push back: these aren’t the words of a madman — and can a demon give sight to the blind?

f.w: Can a devil open the eyes of the blind?

chapters.n: Some months later it is winter, during the Feast of Dedication in Jerusalem — the holiday now called Hanukkah.

f.g: Celebrated the rededication of the temple in 164 BC after the Maccabees drove out the Syrian king who had defiled it.

chapters.n: Jesus walks in Solomon’s Porch, a covered colonnade on the east side of the temple courts, sheltered from the winter weather.
The leaders surround him and demand that he stop keeping them in suspense: if he is the Messiah, he should say so plainly.

f.w: How long dost thou make us to doubt?
f.g: Literally “How long will you hold our souls in suspense?”

chapters.n: Jesus says he has already told them, and his miracles done in his Father’s name testify of him.

f.w: the works that I do in my Father's name

chapters.n: Their unbelief shows they are not among his sheep.

f.w: ye are not of my sheep

chapters.n: His true sheep listen to his voice, he knows them, and they follow him — three marks of genuine discipleship.
He gives them eternal life, and no one can snatch them out of his hand. Though we can choose to walk away, no outside power can tear us from Christ.

f.w: neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand

chapters.n: The Father who gave them to him is greater than all, and no one can snatch them from the Father’s hand either.
“I and my Father are one.” Latter-day Saints understand this as perfect unity of purpose, will, and love between two distinct beings — the same oneness Jesus later prays his disciples will share.

f.w: I and my Father are one
f.g: In Greek “one” is neuter (hen) — one in essence or purpose, not one person.

chapters.n: Taking his words as a claim to divinity, the leaders again pick up stones to kill him.
Jesus calmly asks which of the many good works he has shown them from his Father they are stoning him for.

f.g: shewed = showed.

chapters.n: They reply that it’s not for a good deed but for blasphemy: he, a man, is making himself God.

f.g: blasphemy = speaking irreverently of God or claiming divine status falsely.

chapters.n: Jesus quotes Psalm 82, where God calls human judges “gods.”

f.g: Here “law” means the scriptures generally, not only the five books of Moses.

chapters.n: If scripture — which cannot be set aside — calls those who received God’s word “gods,” the title can’t automatically be blasphemy.
How much more fitting, then, for the one the Father set apart and sent into the world to call himself the Son of God.

f.g: sanctified = set apart as holy for a sacred purpose.

chapters.n: If Jesus isn’t doing his Father’s works, they shouldn’t believe him. He welcomes being tested by his deeds.
But if he is doing them, even those who struggle to believe his words should believe the evidence of his works, and so come to know that the Father is in him and he in the Father.

f.w: the Father is in me, and I in him

chapters.n: They try to arrest him again, but he slips out of their grasp.

f.w: he escaped out of their hand

chapters.n: Jesus withdraws across the Jordan to Bethabara, where John the Baptist had first baptized, and stays there — a place full of memories of the beginning of his ministry.
Many come to him and say that, although John performed no miracles, everything he said about Jesus proved true. A faithful witness’s words outlast him.
Many people there come to believe in him — a quiet harvest from John the Baptist’s earlier preaching.
John introduces Lazarus of Bethany, the brother of Mary and Martha — close friends of Jesus. Bethany was a village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives.

f.g: A form of the Hebrew Eleazar, “God has helped.”

chapters.n: John identifies this Mary as the one who anointed Jesus’s feet and wiped them with her hair — an event he will narrate in the next chapter, assuming his readers already know the story.
The sisters send a simple message: “Lord, the one you love is sick.” They don’t demand anything; they trust his love to act.

f.g: Some have suggested Lazarus may be the unnamed “beloved disciple,” but most identify that disciple as John.

chapters.n: Jesus says the sickness won’t end in death but will bring glory to God and to the Son. Lazarus will die, but death won’t have the last word.
John emphasizes that Jesus truly loved Martha, Mary, and Lazarus — so his delay that follows is not indifference.

f.g: John uses agapaō here, the word for deep, committed love.

chapters.n: Yet Jesus waits two more days where he is. Sometimes divine delays serve a greater purpose than an immediate answer would.
Then he tells the disciples they will go back to Judea.

f.g: The southern region containing Jerusalem and Bethany.

chapters.n: The disciples are alarmed: the leaders there just tried to stone him. Why go back?
Jesus answers with a proverb: there are twelve hours of daylight; someone walking by day doesn’t stumble because they can see. His day of work isn’t over yet.

f.g: Daylight was divided into twelve hours, varying in length with the seasons.

chapters.n: Stumbling happens in the dark, when one has no light. Walking with Christ is walking in the light.

f.w: there is no light in him

chapters.n: Jesus says their friend Lazarus has “fallen asleep,” and he is going to wake him.

f.g: Early Christians often called death “sleep,” since believers will awake in the Resurrection.

chapters.n: The disciples take him literally: if Lazarus is sleeping, he’ll recover.

f.g: Literally “he will be saved” — he will get better.

chapters.n: John explains the misunderstanding: Jesus meant death, but they thought he meant ordinary rest.

f.g: Howbeit = however.

chapters.n: So Jesus tells them plainly: Lazarus is dead.

f.g: Jesus knew this without being told.

chapters.n: He is glad, for their sake, that he wasn’t there to prevent it, because what they are about to see will strengthen their faith.

f.w: to the intent ye may believe

chapters.n: Thomas, called “the Twin,” bravely urges the others to go along and die with Jesus. Remembered as a doubter, he here shows courageous loyalty.

f.g: Greek for “twin,” the same meaning as the Aramaic name Thomas.

f.w: that we may die with him

chapters.n: When Jesus arrives, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Some Jews believed the soul lingered near the body for three days, so by day four death seemed final.

f.g: The detail stresses that Lazarus was truly and irreversibly dead by human standards.

chapters.n: Bethany was close to Jerusalem — about two miles away.

f.g: About 1¾ to 2 miles (roughly 3 km).

chapters.n: Many people from Jerusalem had come to comfort the sisters, as Jewish mourning customs encouraged.

f.g: Mourning traditionally lasted seven days, with friends visiting the grieving family.

chapters.n: Martha, ever the active one, hurries out to meet Jesus, while Mary stays seated in the house, perhaps overwhelmed by grief.

f.w: Mary sat still in the house
f.g: Mourners customarily sat on the floor.

chapters.n: Martha speaks with honest grief: if Jesus had been there, her brother wouldn’t have died.

f.g: Both sisters say exactly the same words (verse 32) — they had surely said it to each other many times.

chapters.n: Yet her faith shines through: even now, she knows God will give Jesus whatever he asks.
Jesus promises her that her brother will rise again.
Martha takes this as the familiar comfort that Lazarus will rise at the final resurrection, a doctrine the Pharisees taught.

f.w: the resurrection at the last day

chapters.n: Jesus brings the doctrine into the present: he himself is the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in him will live, even after dying.

f.w: I am the resurrection, and the life

chapters.n: And whoever lives believing in him will never truly die. Then he asks her directly, “Do you believe this?”

f.g: Jesus invites a personal testimony, not just agreement with a doctrine.

chapters.n: Martha answers with a full confession of faith: Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, the one who was to come into the world — a testimony equal to Peter’s.

f.w: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God

chapters.n: Martha quietly goes to fetch Mary, telling her privately that the Teacher has come and is asking for her.

f.w: The Master is come, and calleth for thee

chapters.n: Mary gets up at once and goes to him.

f.g: Her quick response shows her devotion despite her grief.

chapters.n: Jesus is still outside the village where Martha met him, perhaps to see the sisters away from the crowd.

f.w: not yet come into the town
f.g: Possibly near the tomb, which would have been outside the village.

chapters.n: The mourners in the house see Mary rush out and follow, assuming she is going to the tomb to weep.

f.g: Visiting the tomb to mourn was customary during the days after burial.

chapters.n: Mary falls at Jesus’s feet — where she is always found in the Gospels — and repeats the same heartbroken words as Martha.

f.w: she fell down at his feet

chapters.n: Seeing Mary and the others weeping, Jesus is deeply moved and stirred within. The Greek suggests intense emotion — perhaps even indignation at death and the sorrow it causes.

f.g: Greek embrimaomai — to be deeply moved, to snort with strong emotion.

chapters.n: He asks where they have buried Lazarus, and they invite him to “come and see.”
The shortest verse in the Bible: Jesus wept. Even knowing he would raise Lazarus within minutes, he shared their grief. Christ does not stand apart from our sorrow.
Onlookers are touched by how much he loved Lazarus.
Others wonder why the man who healed the blind couldn’t have kept his friend from dying — a question many grieving people still ask.

f.w: which opened the eyes of the blind

chapters.n: Deeply moved again, Jesus comes to the tomb — a cave with a large stone across its entrance.

f.w: It was a cave, and a stone lay upon it
f.g: Wealthier families used rock-cut tombs sealed with heavy stones.

chapters.n: Jesus orders the stone removed. Practical Martha objects: after four days, the smell will be terrible.

f.g: Bodies were not embalmed; decay would be well underway.

chapters.n: Jesus reminds her of his promise: if she believes, she will see God’s glory.

f.w: thou shouldest see the glory of God

chapters.n: They roll away the stone. Jesus looks up and thanks his Father for already hearing him — giving thanks before the miracle is visible.

f.w: Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me

chapters.n: Jesus knows the Father always hears him; he prays aloud so the onlookers will believe the Father sent him.
Then with a loud voice he commands: “Lazarus, come out!” One day his voice will call all the dead from their graves.

The dead man walks out, still wrapped in burial cloths, his face covered with a cloth. Jesus tells them to unwrap him and set him free. Lazarus was restored to mortal life; he would die again someday, unlike Jesus in his resurrection.

f.g: Strips of linen wound around the body with spices.
napkin = a cloth used to cover the face.

f.w: Loose him, and let him go
f.g: Some see a picture of how Christ frees us from the bonds of sin and death.

chapters.n: Many of the mourners who saw this put their faith in Jesus.
But some go and report the miracle to the Pharisees — a sign that evidence alone doesn’t change hearts.

f.w: went their ways to the Pharisees

chapters.n: The chief priests and Pharisees call a meeting of the Sanhedrin. They admit Jesus is doing many miracles — yet ask only what they should do about it.

f.g: The Sanhedrin, the 71-member supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Their fear is political: if everyone believes in him, the Romans might see a messianic uprising and destroy the temple (“our place”) and the nation.

f.w: take away both our place and nation
f.g: Ironically, the Romans did destroy the temple and Jerusalem in AD 70.

chapters.n: Caiaphas, high priest that year, speaks bluntly and rudely to the council: they understand nothing.

f.g: High priest from about AD 18 to 36, son-in-law of Annas.

chapters.n: His cold logic: better for one man to die than for the whole nation to be destroyed.

f.g: expedient = advantageous, in one’s interest.

chapters.n: John sees divine irony: without realizing it, Caiaphas, by virtue of his office, prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation — words true in a far deeper sense than he intended.
And Jesus would die not only for Israel but to gather God’s scattered children everywhere into one.

f.w: gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad

chapters.n: From that day the leaders formally plot to put Jesus to death. Giving life to Lazarus seals Jesus’s own death sentence.

f.w: took counsel together for to put him to death

chapters.n: Jesus stops moving openly in Judea and withdraws with his disciples to a town called Ephraim, near the wilderness north of Jerusalem.

f.g: Probably modern et-Taiyibeh, about 12–15 miles northeast of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: The Passover is near, and many pilgrims come to Jerusalem early to complete purification rites before the feast.
Standing in the temple, people look for Jesus and speculate whether he will dare come to the festival.

f.w: he will not come to the feast?

chapters.n: The chief priests and Pharisees have ordered anyone who knows his whereabouts to report it so they can arrest him. The stage is set for his final Passover.

f.g: shew = show, report.

chapters.n: Six days before Passover, Jesus returns to Bethany, home of the recently raised Lazarus. The countdown to the cross has begun.

f.g: Likely the Saturday before the crucifixion week, by the usual reckoning.

chapters.n: A dinner is held in his honor. True to form, Martha serves, and Lazarus — alive again — reclines at the table with Jesus.

f.g: Matthew and Mark place the meal at the house of Simon the leper.

chapters.n: Mary pours a pound of expensive perfume on Jesus’s feet and wipes them with her hair. The fragrance fills the house — an extravagant act of love and humility.

f.g: An aromatic oil from a plant grown in the Himalayas, imported at great cost.

f.w: wiped his feet with her hair
f.g: A respectable woman rarely let down her hair in public; Mary sets aside pride to honor him.

chapters.n: Judas Iscariot, the disciple who would betray Jesus, objects.
He complains that the perfume could have been sold for three hundred denarii — about a year’s wages — and the money given to the poor.

f.g: 300 denarii, roughly a year’s pay for a laborer.

chapters.n: John reveals Judas’s real motive: he didn’t care about the poor. He kept the group’s money bag and stole from it.

f.g: bag = the common money box; bare = carried off, pilfered.

chapters.n: Jesus defends Mary: leave her alone. Whether she fully knew it or not, she was preparing his body for burial.

f.w: against the day of my burying
f.g: against = in preparation for.

chapters.n: There will always be chances to help the poor, but Jesus would not be with them much longer. He isn’t dismissing the poor; he is pointing to the uniqueness of this moment.

f.w: the poor always ye have with you

chapters.n: A large crowd hears he is in Bethany and comes — not only to see Jesus but also to see Lazarus, the man raised from the dead.

f.w: that they might see Lazarus also
f.g: Lazarus was living proof of Jesus’s power.

chapters.n: The chief priests then plot to kill Lazarus as well — a chilling sign of how far they would go to stop belief in Jesus.

f.g: Most chief priests were Sadducees, who denied the resurrection; a raised man was doubly inconvenient.

chapters.n: Because of Lazarus, many people are leaving the leaders’ influence and believing in Jesus.

f.w: went away, and believed on Jesus

chapters.n: The next day — Palm Sunday — the festival crowds hear Jesus is coming to Jerusalem.
They wave palm branches, a symbol of victory and national hope, and shout “Hosanna!” — hailing him as the King of Israel who comes in the Lord’s name.

f.g: Hebrew “save now, we pray” — a plea that became a shout of praise.

chapters.n: Jesus deliberately rides in on a young donkey, fulfilling prophecy. A king on a donkey came in peace, not on a war horse.

f.g: ass = donkey.

chapters.n: John quotes Zechariah: Zion need not fear, for her King comes riding on a donkey’s colt — a humble, peaceful king.

f.g: Sion = Zion, a poetic name for Jerusalem and its people.

chapters.n: At first the disciples didn’t grasp what was happening. Only after Jesus was glorified did they connect the events to scripture.

f.w: when Jesus was glorified, then remembered they

chapters.n: Those who had witnessed Lazarus raised kept telling others about it.

f.g: bare record = testified, bore witness.

chapters.n: That testimony is why so many came out to greet him.

f.g: Literally “this sign” — the climactic sign of John’s Gospel.

chapters.n: The frustrated Pharisees admit their efforts are useless: “the world has gone after him.” Unknowingly they foretell the worldwide reach of his gospel.

f.w: the world is gone after him

chapters.n: Among the pilgrims are some Greeks — Gentiles who worshipped Israel’s God — who had come up to worship at the feast.

f.g: Probably “God-fearers”: non-Jews who worshipped the God of Israel without full conversion.

chapters.n: They approach Philip (who had a Greek name and came from bilingual Bethsaida) with a timeless request: “Sir, we would see Jesus.”

f.g: would = wish to, want to.

chapters.n: Philip consults Andrew, and together they bring the request to Jesus.
The arrival of Gentile seekers signals to Jesus that his “hour” — the time of his death and glorification — has now come.
Jesus explains with a farming image: a grain of wheat must be buried and die to produce a harvest. His death will bring forth abundant life.

f.g: corn = a single grain or kernel.

chapters.n: The same principle applies to disciples: clinging to this life loses it; giving it up for God preserves it forever.

f.w: He that loveth his life shall lose it
f.g: “Hate” here is a Semitic way of saying “love less by comparison.”

chapters.n: Serving Christ means following him — even to the cross — and the Father will honor those who serve him.

f.w: where I am, there shall also my servant be

chapters.n: Jesus is troubled at what lies ahead. Should he ask to be spared? No — this is the very reason he came. This is John’s version of the anguish of Gethsemane.
His prayer is simply, “Father, glorify thy name.” A voice from heaven answers: the Father has glorified it and will again.
Some bystanders think it thundered; others say an angel spoke. People heard the same voice differently according to their readiness.
Jesus explains that the voice came for their benefit, not his.
Now judgment comes upon the world, and Satan, its “prince,” will be driven out. Christ’s death and resurrection will break the devil’s hold.
When he is lifted up from the earth on the cross, he will draw all people to himself.

f.w: will draw all men unto me

chapters.n: John explains: “lifted up” pointed to the kind of death he would die — crucifixion.
The crowd is confused: scripture says the Messiah remains forever. How can the Son of Man be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?
Rather than debate, Jesus urges them: the light is with them only a little longer, so walk in it before darkness overtakes them.

f.w: Walk while ye have the light

chapters.n: Believe in the light while you have it, and become children of light. Then Jesus withdraws from public view.
John reflects sadly that despite all of Jesus’s signs, many still would not believe in him.

f.g: John has recorded seven major signs in chapters 2–11.

chapters.n: This fulfilled Isaiah’s words about Israel’s unbelief: “Lord, who has believed our report?” — words from the great chapter about the suffering servant.

f.w: Lord, who hath believed our report?
f.g: Esaias = the Greek form of Isaiah.

chapters.n: John adds a second prophecy from Isaiah explaining their failure to believe.

Isaiah foresaw people whose eyes were blinded and hearts hardened. Scripture often describes the result of persistent rejection as if God caused it; people who repeatedly refuse light lose the capacity to see.
Isaiah said this because he saw Jesus’s glory. John identifies the Lord Isaiah saw on the throne in the temple as the premortal Christ.
Still, even many leaders privately believed in Jesus, but feared to confess it lest the Pharisees have them expelled from the synagogue.

f.w: chief rulers also many believed on him

chapters.n: The root problem: they loved human approval more than God’s approval.
Jesus cries out a final public summary: believing in him is believing in the Father who sent him.

f.w: believeth not on me, but on him that sent me

chapters.n: To see Jesus is to see the Father who sent him — the Son perfectly reflects the Father.

f.w: he that seeth me seeth him that sent me

chapters.n: He has come as light so that no believer need stay in darkness.

f.w: I am come a light into the world

chapters.n: He did not come to condemn people who hear but don’t believe; his purpose is to save the world.

f.w: I came not to judge the world, but to save the world

chapters.n: Yet rejecting him has consequences: the very words he spoke will stand as the judge at the last day.

f.w: the word that I have spoken, the same shall judge him

chapters.n: Jesus did not speak on his own authority; the Father commanded what he should say.
The Father’s commandment leads to eternal life, so Jesus speaks exactly as the Father directs. These words close Jesus’s public ministry in John.
John opens the story of the Last Supper with its theme: knowing his hour had come to leave the world and return to the Father, Jesus loved his own to the very end — to the uttermost.

f.w: he loved them unto the end
f.g: The Greek can mean both “to the end of his life” and “completely, to the fullest.”

chapters.n: During the evening meal, the devil has already planted in Judas’s heart the plan to betray Jesus.

f.g: Better “during supper,” as the meal continues in verse 26.

f.w: put into the heart of Judas

chapters.n: Jesus acts from full awareness of who he is: the Father has given him all things; he came from God and is returning to God. His service flows from that secure identity.

f.w: the Father had given all things into his hands

chapters.n: He gets up from the meal, takes off his outer robe, and ties a towel around his waist — dressing as the lowest household servant.

f.g: girded = tied around the waist, like a servant’s apron.

chapters.n: He pours water into a basin and begins washing and drying the disciples’ dusty feet — a menial task usually left to servants.

f.w: began to wash the disciples' feet
f.g: In the latter days the Lord restored the washing of feet as an ordinance for the School of the Prophets.

chapters.n: When Jesus reaches Peter, Peter is shocked: “Lord, are you going to wash my feet?”

f.g: In Greek, “you” and “my” sit side by side for emphasis: “You — my feet?”

chapters.n: Jesus tells him he won’t understand now, but he will later.
Peter flatly refuses. Jesus answers that unless Peter lets him wash him, Peter can have no part with him. Accepting Christ’s cleansing service is essential.

f.w: thou hast no part with me

chapters.n: Impulsive Peter swings the other way: then wash my hands and head too!

f.g: Typical Peter — all or nothing, wholehearted but not yet understanding.

chapters.n: Jesus explains that one who has bathed only needs his feet washed; they are clean — except one. The JST adds that this was a custom under the law, and Jesus did it to fulfill the law.

f.g: A guest bathed at home and needed only his feet washed after walking to the meal.

f.w: ye are clean, but not all

chapters.n: He said “not all” because he knew who would betray him.
Having finished, Jesus puts his robe back on, returns to the table, and asks if they understand what he has done.

f.w: Know ye what I have done to you?
f.g: A teaching question inviting them to reflect.

chapters.n: They rightly call him Teacher and Lord — and he truly is.

f.g: Master = teacher (rabbi); Lord = one with authority.

chapters.n: If their Lord and Teacher washes their feet, they ought to serve one another in the same humble way.
He has given them an example to follow — leadership through lowly service.

f.w: I have given you an example

chapters.n: A servant isn’t greater than his master, nor a messenger greater than the one who sent him. If Jesus serves, no disciple is too important to serve.

f.w: The servant is not greater than his lord

chapters.n: Knowing this isn’t enough; joy comes from doing it.

f.w: happy are ye if ye do them
f.g: happy = blessed.

chapters.n: Jesus excludes one: he knows whom he chose, but scripture must be fulfilled — someone who shared his bread has turned against him.

f.w: lifted up his heel against me
f.g: To show someone the heel was an insulting gesture of contempt or betrayal.

chapters.n: He tells them in advance so that when it happens, their faith will be strengthened rather than shattered.

f.g: Again the Greek egō eimi, “I am.”

chapters.n: Whoever receives the messengers Jesus sends receives him, and whoever receives him receives the Father. Despite the betrayal, the apostles’ mission stands.

f.w: He that receiveth whomsoever I send receiveth me

chapters.n: Deeply troubled, Jesus declares solemnly that one of the Twelve will betray him.
The disciples look at one another, baffled about whom he means.

f.g: doubting = uncertain, at a loss.

chapters.n: Reclining next to Jesus is “the disciple whom Jesus loved,” traditionally understood to be John himself, the Gospel’s author.

f.g: Guests reclined on their left side on couches, so the one to Jesus’s right could lean back against his chest.

chapters.n: Peter signals to him to ask Jesus who it is.

f.g: beckoned = signaled with a gesture or nod.

chapters.n: Leaning back against Jesus, the beloved disciple quietly asks, “Lord, who is it?”

f.g: The closeness of the image suggests intimate friendship.

chapters.n: Jesus says it’s the one to whom he gives a piece of bread dipped in the dish — then hands it to Judas. Offering such a morsel was a gesture of honor and friendship, a final appeal.

f.g: sop = a piece of bread dipped in sauce.

chapters.n: After the bread, Satan enters Judas. Jesus tells him, “What you are doing, do quickly.” Judas has made his choice.
No one else at the table understands what Jesus meant.

f.w: no man at the table knew
f.g: Even after the sign, the disciples failed to grasp it.

chapters.n: Since Judas held the money bag, some thought Jesus was sending him to buy supplies for the feast or give to the poor.

f.g: Giving to the poor was customary on Passover night.

chapters.n: Judas takes the bread and leaves at once. John adds four haunting words: “and it was night” — darkness outside and in.
Once Judas is gone, Jesus announces that the Son of Man is now glorified, and God is glorified in him. The path to the cross is now set.

f.w: Now is the Son of man glorified

chapters.n: And God will glorify the Son in himself, and do it soon — through the Resurrection and Ascension.

f.g: straightway = immediately, at once.

chapters.n: Tenderly calling them “little children,” Jesus says he will be with them only a short while; they cannot come where he is going.

f.g: The only place in the Gospels Jesus uses this affectionate term.

chapters.n: He gives a new commandment: love one another as he has loved them. The command to love was old; the new standard is Christ’s own self-giving love.
This love will be the identifying mark of his disciples before the whole world.

f.w: By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples

chapters.n: Peter, still stuck on Jesus leaving, asks where he is going. Jesus says Peter can’t follow now but will later — a hint at Peter’s own future martyrdom.
Peter protests: why not now? He will lay down his life for Jesus!

f.w: I will lay down my life for thy sake

chapters.n: Jesus gently questions his confidence and foretells that before the rooster crows, Peter will deny him three times. Peter’s love is real; his strength is not yet.

f.w: The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice
f.g: thrice = three times.

chapters.n: Still at the Last Supper, Jesus comforts his anxious disciples: don’t let your hearts be troubled. You trust God — trust me too.

f.w: Let not your heart be troubled

chapters.n: His Father’s house has many dwelling places, and he is going ahead to prepare one for them. Latter-day revelation teaches that heaven has many kingdoms and degrees of glory.

f.g: mansions = dwelling places, rooms (Greek monai).

chapters.n: Having prepared a place, he will come again and take them to himself, so they can be where he is. His goal is to be together with them forever.
He tells them they already know the way to where he is going.

f.g: They know the way because they know him (verse 6).

chapters.n: Honest Thomas speaks up: they don’t even know where he’s going, so how could they know the way?
Jesus answers with one of his most famous statements: he himself is the Way, the Truth, and the Life. No one reaches the Father except through him.

f.w: I am the way, the truth, and the life

chapters.n: Knowing Jesus means knowing the Father. From now on, he says, they do know the Father and have seen him — in the Son.

f.w: ye should have known my Father also

chapters.n: Philip asks Jesus simply to show them the Father — that would be enough for them.

f.g: suffice = be enough.

chapters.n: Gently but with some sadness, Jesus asks whether Philip still doesn’t know him after all this time. Anyone who has seen Jesus has seen what the Father is like — his character, love, and will.

f.w: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father

chapters.n: The Father and the Son dwell in each other in perfect unity; Jesus’s words and works are the Father’s.

f.w: I am in the Father, and the Father in me

chapters.n: Believe his word about that unity — or if that’s hard, believe because of the works he does.
Those who believe in him will do the works he does — and even greater ones — because he is going to the Father and will send the Spirit. His disciples would spread the gospel across the world.

f.w: greater works than these shall he do

chapters.n: Whatever they ask in his name he will do, so that the Father is glorified through the Son. Praying “in his name” means asking in harmony with his will and character.

f.w: whatsoever ye shall ask in my name

chapters.n: Jesus repeats the promise for emphasis.

f.w: If ye shall ask any thing in my name

chapters.n: Love for Christ is shown by keeping his commandments — obedience is love in action.

f.w: If ye love me, keep my commandments

chapters.n: Jesus will ask the Father to send them “another Comforter” to be with them forever. While Jesus had been their comforter in person, the Holy Ghost will now take that role.

f.g: Greek paraklētos — one called alongside to help: advocate, counselor, encourager.

chapters.n: This Comforter is the Spirit of truth. The world can’t receive him because it neither sees nor knows him, but the disciples know him, for he is with them and will be in them.
He will not leave them as orphans; he will come to them — after his resurrection, through the Spirit, and in personal visitations.

f.g: Literally “orphans.”

chapters.n: Soon the world will no longer see him, but they will. Because he lives, they too will live — his resurrection guarantees theirs.

f.w: because I live, ye shall live also

chapters.n: In that day they will understand the deep unity between the Father and the Son, and between Christ and his disciples.

f.w: ye in me, and I in you

chapters.n: Whoever keeps his commandments truly loves him, will be loved by the Father, and Jesus will love him and reveal himself to him.
Another Judas — not Iscariot, probably the apostle also called Thaddeus — asks why Jesus will reveal himself to them but not to the whole world.

f.w: Judas saith unto him, not Iscariot

chapters.n: Jesus answers that the Father and the Son will come and make their home with anyone who loves him and keeps his word. Latter-day revelation teaches that this describes a personal appearance of the Father and the Son.

f.w: we will come unto him, and make our abode with him
f.g: abode = dwelling, home.

chapters.n: Those who don’t love him don’t keep his words — and those words come from the Father.

f.w: is not mine, but the Father's which sent me

chapters.n: He has told them these things while still with them in person.

f.g: A hint that his physical presence is about to end.

chapters.n: After he leaves, the Holy Ghost, sent by the Father in Jesus’s name, will teach them everything and bring back to their memory all Jesus said. This promise underlies the Gospel writers’ inspired recollection.

f.w: the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost
bring all things to your remembrance

chapters.n: His parting gift is peace — his own peace, not the shallow, temporary peace the world offers. So they need not be troubled or afraid.

f.w: my peace I give unto you

chapters.n: If they truly loved him, they would be glad he is returning to the Father, for the Father is greater than he is. The Father and the Son are distinct, and the Son honors the Father as his superior.

f.w: my Father is greater than I

chapters.n: He tells them in advance so that when these events happen, their faith will hold.

f.w: that, when it is come to pass, ye might believe

chapters.n: He won’t talk much longer, for the “prince of this world” — Satan — is coming. But Satan has no hold or claim on Jesus at all.

f.g: Satan has no foothold — no sin or weakness in Jesus to grab onto.

chapters.n: Jesus goes to the cross to show the world his love for the Father and his perfect obedience. Then he says, “Get up, let’s go” — perhaps leaving the upper room, with chapters 15–17 spoken on the way.

f.w: as the Father gave me commandment, even so I do

f.g: hence = from here.

chapters.n: Jesus gives his last great “I am” saying: he is the true vine, and his Father is the gardener who tends it. Israel was often pictured as God’s vine; Jesus is the faithful one.

f.g: husbandman = farmer, vinedresser.

chapters.n: The gardener removes branches that bear no fruit and prunes the fruitful ones so they bear even more. Pruning hurts, but it makes us more productive.

f.g: purge = prune, cleanse. The Greek words for “prune” and “clean” (v. 3) are related.

f.w: that it may bring forth more fruit

chapters.n: The disciples have already been made clean through the word Jesus has spoken to them.
“Abide in me” — stay connected. A branch can’t produce fruit cut off from the vine, and neither can disciples apart from Christ.

f.w: Abide in me, and I in you
f.g: abide = remain, stay, dwell.

chapters.n: He is the vine; they are the branches. Connected to him they bear much fruit; without him they can do nothing of eternal worth.

f.w: without me ye can do nothing

chapters.n: Branches that don’t stay connected wither and are gathered for burning — a sober warning about cutting ourselves off from Christ.
When we abide in him and his words abide in us, our desires align with his, and we can ask what we will and receive it.

f.w: ye shall ask what ye will

chapters.n: The Father is glorified when disciples bear abundant fruit; this is how they show they are truly his disciples.
Jesus loves them as the Father loves him. He invites them to remain in that love.
Keeping his commandments keeps them in his love — just as Jesus keeps his Father’s commandments and remains in his love.
He has told them these things so his joy will be in them and their joy will be complete.

f.w: that your joy might be full

chapters.n: His commandment: love one another as he has loved them.
The greatest love is to lay down one’s life for one’s friends — exactly what Jesus is about to do.

f.w: Greater love hath no man than this

chapters.n: They are his friends when they do what he commands.
He no longer calls them servants, who are kept in the dark, but friends — because he has shared with them everything he heard from his Father.
They didn’t choose him; he chose and ordained them to go out and bear fruit that lasts. Their calling came from him.

f.w: I have chosen you, and ordained you

chapters.n: He sums up all these instructions with one command: love one another.
Turning to the coming opposition: if the world hates them, they should remember it hated him first.
If they belonged to the world, it would love them as its own. Because Jesus chose them out of it, the world hates them.

f.w: ye are not of the world

chapters.n: He reminds them that a servant isn’t greater than his master. If people persecuted him, they will persecute his disciples; if they kept his word, they will keep theirs.

f.w: The servant is not greater than his lord

chapters.n: They will suffer all this for his name’s sake, because their persecutors don’t know the Father who sent him.
Had Jesus not come and taught them, they would not be guilty of rejecting him; now they have no excuse.

f.g: cloak = covering, excuse.

chapters.n: To hate Jesus is to hate the Father who sent him.
His unique miracles left them without excuse. They have seen and still hated both him and the Father.

f.w: the works which none other man did

chapters.n: This fulfilled the scriptures: “They hated me without a cause.”

f.w: They hated me without a cause

f.g: Again meaning the scriptures as a whole, here the Psalms.

chapters.n: But when the Comforter comes — the Spirit of truth whom Jesus will send from the Father — he will testify of Jesus.
And the disciples, who have been with him from the start, will also bear witness. The Spirit’s testimony and theirs will work together.
Jesus explains why he is warning them in advance: so they won’t stumble and fall away when persecution comes.

f.g: offended = caused to stumble, to lose faith.

chapters.n: They will be thrown out of synagogues, and some who kill them will even think they are serving God. Saul of Tarsus would be one such persecutor before his conversion.

f.w: put you out of the synagogues
will think that he doeth God service

chapters.n: Persecutors act this way because they don’t truly know the Father or the Son.

f.w: they have not known the Father

chapters.n: He tells them now so they will remember his warning when it happens. He hadn’t mentioned it earlier because he was with them to protect them.

f.w: ye may remember that I told you

chapters.n: He is returning to the Father who sent him, yet none of them are asking where he’s going — they’re focused on their own loss.

f.g: Peter and Thomas had asked earlier (13:36; 14:5), but now grief has silenced them.

chapters.n: Because of what he has told them, sorrow has filled their hearts.
Still, it is for their good that he leaves, for only then will the Comforter come. The Holy Ghost could be a constant companion to every disciple everywhere.

f.w: It is expedient for you that I go away
f.g: expedient = beneficial, to your advantage.

chapters.n: When the Comforter comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment — showing people the truth about themselves and about Christ.

f.g: reprove = convict, expose, prove wrong.

chapters.n: Concerning sin: the deepest sin is refusing to believe in Christ.
Concerning righteousness: Jesus’s return to the Father vindicates him as the Righteous One, even though the world condemned him.
Concerning judgment: Satan, the ruler of this world, has already been judged and defeated by Christ’s victory.

f.w: the prince of this world is judged

chapters.n: There is much more he could teach, but they cannot handle it yet. Revelation comes line upon line, as we are ready.
The Spirit of truth will guide them into all truth. He won’t speak on his own but will speak what he hears, and will reveal things to come.

f.w: he will guide you into all truth
he will shew you things to come

chapters.n: The Spirit will glorify Jesus by taking what is his and making it known to them. The Holy Ghost always points to Christ.
Everything the Father has belongs to the Son too, so what the Spirit reveals from the Son comes from the Father as well. Father, Son, and Holy Ghost work in perfect unity.

f.w: All things that the Father hath are mine

chapters.n: In a little while they won’t see him (at his death), and then in a little while they will see him again (at his resurrection).
Some disciples puzzle among themselves over his words about “a little while” and going to the Father.

f.w: What is this that he saith unto us
f.g: Their repeated confusion is honest and relatable.

chapters.n: They keep repeating the phrase, admitting they don’t understand.

f.w: we cannot tell what he saith
f.g: cannot tell = don’t know.

chapters.n: Jesus senses they want to ask and raises the question for them.

f.w: Jesus knew that they were desirous to ask him

chapters.n: They will weep and mourn while the world celebrates his death, but their grief will be turned into joy.

f.w: your sorrow shall be turned into joy

chapters.n: Like a woman in labor, whose pain is forgotten in the joy of her newborn, their anguish will give way to joy when new life comes.

f.g: travail = labor pains of childbirth.

chapters.n: They are sorrowful now, but he will see them again, their hearts will rejoice, and no one will be able to take that joy away.

f.w: your joy no man taketh from you

chapters.n: In that day they won’t need to ask him questions as before; they may pray directly to the Father in Jesus’s name, and the Father will give it. This is why we pray to the Father in Christ’s name.

f.w: Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name

chapters.n: Until now they haven’t prayed in his name. Now they should ask and receive, so their joy may be full.
He has been using figures of speech, but the time is coming when he will speak plainly about the Father.

f.g: proverbs = figures of speech, veiled sayings.

chapters.n: In that day they will ask in his name. Jesus does not mean he stops interceding, but that they will have direct access to the Father.

f.w: I will pray the Father for you

chapters.n: The Father himself loves them because they have loved Jesus and believed he came from God.
Jesus summarizes his whole mission in one sentence: he came from the Father into the world, and now leaves the world to return to the Father.

f.w: I came forth from the Father

chapters.n: The disciples say that now he is speaking plainly, not in figures.

f.g: Lo = look, see.

chapters.n: They declare their confidence that he knows all things and that he came from God.
Jesus asks, perhaps with gentle irony, “Do you believe now?” Their faith is real but about to be tested.

f.g: Could also be read as a statement: “Now you believe” — yet trials are coming.

chapters.n: The hour has come when they will scatter and leave him alone. Yet he is not alone, because the Father is with him.
His final word before his prayer: in him they can have peace. The world will bring troubles, but take heart — he has overcome the world.

Jesus looks up to heaven and prays. This chapter, often called the Intercessory Prayer, is the longest recorded prayer of Jesus. He begins: the hour has come — glorify your Son so the Son can glorify you.

f.w: lifted up his eyes to heaven

chapters.n: The Father has given the Son authority over all humanity so that he can give eternal life to those the Father has given him.
Jesus defines eternal life: to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. It is not just endless existence but a personal, growing relationship with the Father and the Son.

f.w: this is life eternal, that they might know thee

chapters.n: Jesus reports to his Father that he has glorified him on earth and finished the work he was given — speaking with confidence even before the cross.
He asks to be restored to the glory he shared with the Father before the world was created — a clear statement of his premortal existence.

f.w: the glory which I had with thee before the world was

chapters.n: He has revealed the Father’s name — his true nature — to the disciples given him out of the world. They belonged to the Father, he gave them to Jesus, and they have kept God’s word.

f.g: In Hebrew thought, a “name” stands for a person’s character and identity.

chapters.n: They now understand that everything Jesus has comes from the Father.
He gave them the Father’s words; they received them and know for sure that he came from the Father.
Here he prays specifically for his disciples, who belong to the Father.

f.w: I pray not for the world
f.g: Not a rejection of the world (see verse 21), but focused intercession for these disciples now.

chapters.n: All that is his is the Father’s and all that is the Father’s is his, and he is glorified in his disciples.

f.w: all mine are thine, and thine are mine

chapters.n: As he leaves the world, he asks the Holy Father to protect the disciples, keeping them united as the Father and Son are one.

f.w: that they may be one, as we are
f.g: The unity of the disciples is modeled on that of the Father and the Son — unity of heart and purpose.

chapters.n: While with them, Jesus protected them and lost none except the “son of perdition,” Judas, who chose destruction as scripture foretold.

f.g: perdition = ruin, destruction. Here an idiom for one headed to ruin.

chapters.n: Now he is coming to the Father, and he prays aloud so they may have his joy fully in themselves.
He has given them God’s word, and the world hates them, because like him they don’t belong to the world.
He doesn’t ask the Father to remove them from the world, but to protect them from the evil one. Disciples are meant to live in the world without being ruled by it.

f.g: Or “from the evil one,” Satan.

chapters.n: He repeats: they are not of the world, just as he is not.

f.w: They are not of the world

chapters.n: He asks the Father to make them holy through truth — God’s word is truth.

f.g: sanctify = make holy, set apart for God’s purposes.

chapters.n: Just as the Father sent him into the world, he sends them. The word “apostle” means “one who is sent.”

f.w: even so have I also sent them into the world

chapters.n: For their sake he consecrates himself — gives himself entirely as a sacrifice — so they can be made holy through the truth.

f.g: Jesus dedicates himself to the sacrifice he is about to offer.

chapters.n: He widens his prayer to include all who will later believe through the apostles’ testimony — including believers today.

f.w: them also which shall believe on me through their word

chapters.n: He prays that all believers may be one, just as the Father is in him and he in the Father, so the world will believe the Father sent him. Unity among disciples is itself a witness of Christ.

f.w: That they all may be one

chapters.n: He has given them the glory the Father gave him, so they can share that same unity.

f.w: the glory which thou gavest me I have given them

chapters.n: Christ in them and the Father in Christ, so they can be perfected in unity — and the world will know that the Father loves them as he loves his Son.

f.w: hast loved them, as thou hast loved me

chapters.n: His deepest wish: that those given him may be with him where he is and see his glory, given in love before the world’s foundation.

f.w: be with me where I am
before the foundation of the world

chapters.n: Addressing his “righteous Father,” he notes that the world hasn’t known the Father, but he has, and his disciples know the Father sent him.

f.g: Jesus addresses God as Father six times in this prayer.

chapters.n: He has made the Father known and will keep doing so, so that the Father’s love for the Son may be in them, and Christ himself in them.

f.w: the love wherewith thou hast loved me may be in them

chapters.n: After his prayer, Jesus leads the disciples across the Kidron Valley to a garden on the Mount of Olives — Gethsemane, as the other Gospels name it. There he would suffer for the sins of the world.

f.g: The Kidron, a seasonal stream east of Jerusalem; David crossed it weeping when fleeing Absalom.

chapters.n: Judas knew the place because Jesus often went there with his disciples. Jesus didn’t hide; he went where he could be found.

f.g: ofttimes = often; resorted thither = went there.

chapters.n: Judas arrives with a detachment of soldiers and temple police sent by the chief priests and Pharisees, carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons — coming with artificial lights to seize the Light of the World.

f.g: A Roman cohort (or part of one) — showing Roman involvement from the start.

chapters.n: Fully aware of what is coming, Jesus steps forward to meet them and asks, “Who are you looking for?” He is in control, not the mob.

f.w: knowing all things that should come upon him

chapters.n: They say, “Jesus of Nazareth.” He answers, “I am he” — again “I am.” John notes that Judas is standing with the arresting party.

f.g: Greek egō eimi, “I am.”

chapters.n: At his words “I am,” the soldiers draw back and fall to the ground — a brief glimpse of his divine power, even as he submits to arrest.

f.w: they went backward, and fell to the ground

chapters.n: He asks again whom they seek, and again they answer, “Jesus of Nazareth.”
He repeats that he is the one, and asks them to let his disciples go. Even as he is arrested, he protects his own.
This fulfilled his own words in his prayer that he had lost none of those the Father gave him.

f.w: Of them which thou gavest me have I lost none

chapters.n: Peter draws a sword and strikes the high priest’s servant, cutting off his right ear. Only John names the two men — Peter and Malchus.

f.g: Luke adds that Jesus healed the ear.

chapters.n: Jesus tells Peter to put the sword away: shouldn’t he drink the cup the Father has given him? He goes to his suffering willingly.

f.w: the cup which my Father hath given me

chapters.n: The soldiers, their commander, and the temple officers seize Jesus and tie him up.

f.g: Greek chiliarchos — a Roman tribune, commander of about a thousand soldiers.

chapters.n: They take him first to Annas, father-in-law of the current high priest Caiaphas. Annas had been high priest earlier and still held great influence.

f.g: High priest about AD 6–15; five of his sons later held the office as well.

chapters.n: John reminds readers that Caiaphas is the one who advised that one man should die for the people.

f.w: it was expedient that one man should die for the people

chapters.n: Peter follows, along with another disciple — likely John — who knew the high priest and so got into the courtyard with Jesus.

f.g: Unnamed, but often identified with the beloved disciple (John 20:2).
palace = the courtyard of the high priest’s residence.

chapters.n: Peter waits outside the gate until the other disciple speaks to the girl at the door and brings him in.

f.g: A servant girl acting as doorkeeper.

chapters.n: The doorkeeper asks Peter if he’s one of “this man’s” disciples too. Peter says, “I am not” — his first denial, in contrast to Jesus’s “I am.”

f.g: damsel = young woman, servant girl.

chapters.n: It is a cold night, and servants and officers stand around a charcoal fire. Peter stands with them, warming himself — among the very people who arrested Jesus.

f.g: A charcoal fire; John mentions one again in John 21:9, when Peter is restored.

chapters.n: The high priest questions Jesus about his disciples and his teaching, hoping to find something to charge him with.

f.g: doctrine = teaching.

chapters.n: Jesus replies that he has always taught openly in synagogues and the temple; he has said nothing in secret.

f.w: I spake openly to the world

chapters.n: Why question him? Under their own legal practice, witnesses should be heard. Ask those who listened to him.

f.g: Jewish law did not require an accused man to testify against himself; the case should rest on witnesses.

chapters.n: An officer slaps Jesus for speaking that way to the high priest.

f.w: struck Jesus with the palm of his hand

chapters.n: Jesus calmly answers: if he said something wrong, testify to what it was; if not, why strike him? He insists on justice without retaliating.

f.g: smitest = hit, strike.

chapters.n: Annas then sends Jesus, still bound, to Caiaphas the high priest.

f.g: John skips the trial before Caiaphas that the other Gospels record.

chapters.n: Meanwhile Peter is still warming himself by the fire. Asked again if he is a disciple, he denies it a second time.
A relative of Malchus — whose ear Peter cut off — asks if he didn’t see Peter in the garden with Jesus. The danger is very personal now.

f.w: his kinsman whose ear Peter cut off
f.g: kinsman = relative.

chapters.n: Peter denies a third time, and at that moment a rooster crows — just as Jesus foretold.

f.g: Luke adds that Jesus looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.

chapters.n: At dawn they take Jesus from Caiaphas to the Roman governor’s headquarters. The accusers won’t enter a Gentile’s house, to avoid becoming ritually unclean before the Passover meal — careful about ritual while plotting an innocent man’s death.

f.g: The praetorium, the Roman governor’s residence and court in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea, comes out to them and asks what charge they bring.

f.g: Roman prefect of Judea about AD 26–36, known for harsh treatment of the Jews.

chapters.n: They evade the question: if he weren’t a criminal, they wouldn’t have brought him.

f.g: malefactor = evildoer, criminal.

chapters.n: Pilate tells them to judge him by their own law. They reply that they aren’t allowed to execute anyone — revealing that they want him dead.

f.w: It is not lawful for us to put any man to death
f.g: Under Roman rule, the Jewish council generally lacked authority to carry out capital punishment.

chapters.n: This fulfilled Jesus’s own prediction of how he would die: lifted up on a Roman cross, rather than stoned under Jewish law.

f.w: signifying what death he should die

chapters.n: Pilate goes back inside, summons Jesus, and asks, “Are you the King of the Jews?” — the political charge that could mean rebellion against Rome.

f.w: Art thou the King of the Jews?

chapters.n: Jesus asks whether Pilate means this himself or is repeating what others said.

f.w: Sayest thou this thing of thyself
f.g: In effect: is this your question, or theirs?

chapters.n: Pilate scoffs, “Am I a Jew?” His own people and chief priests handed him over — what has he done?

f.g: Pilate distances himself from what he sees as an internal Jewish dispute.

chapters.n: Jesus explains his kingdom isn’t of this world. If it were, his followers would fight to stop his arrest. His is a kingdom of truth and hearts, not armies.

f.w: My kingdom is not of this world

chapters.n: “So you are a king?” Pilate asks. Jesus answers that Pilate has said it, and explains he was born to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who loves truth listens to him.

f.w: To this end was I born
Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice

chapters.n: Pilate asks, “What is truth?” — perhaps cynically — and walks away without waiting for an answer, though Truth stands before him. He then declares Jesus innocent.

f.w: I find in him no fault at all

chapters.n: Pilate reminds them of a Passover custom of releasing one prisoner, and offers to free “the King of the Jews.”
The crowd shouts for Barabbas instead — a robber and insurrectionist. The guilty man goes free while the innocent one is condemned, a picture of what Christ does for us all.

f.g: Aramaic for “son of the father.” Mark and Luke say he took part in a rebellion and committed murder.

chapters.n: Pilate has Jesus flogged, perhaps hoping the punishment will satisfy the crowd. Roman scourging used whips weighted with bone or metal and could kill a man.
The soldiers mock Jesus as a pretend king: they twist thorny branches into a crown and throw a purple robe — the color of royalty — over him.

f.g: Thorns were part of the curse of the Fall; Christ wears them as he removes the curse.
plaited = braided, woven.

chapters.n: They salute him in mockery and strike him repeatedly. Unknowingly, they speak the truth: he is the King.
Pilate brings him out again, insisting he finds no basis for a charge.

f.w: I find no fault in him

chapters.n: Jesus comes out wearing the thorns and purple robe. Pilate says, “Behold the man!” — perhaps meaning “Look at this pitiful man.” John’s readers hear more: here is the true Man, the Son of God.

f.g: In Latin, Ecce homo — a phrase famous in Christian art.

chapters.n: The chief priests and officers scream for crucifixion. Pilate, frustrated, tells them to crucify him themselves, again declaring him innocent.
They reveal their real charge: by their law he deserves death for claiming to be the Son of God.

f.w: he made himself the Son of God

chapters.n: This frightens Pilate even more. Romans told stories of gods walking among men, and perhaps his conscience was stirring.

f.g: Matthew adds that Pilate’s wife warned him because of a dream.

chapters.n: Pilate takes Jesus back inside and asks, “Where are you from?” Jesus gives no answer.
Pilate is irritated: doesn’t Jesus realize Pilate has power to crucify him or set him free?

f.w: I have power to crucify thee
f.g: Pilate thinks he controls the outcome; John shows otherwise.

chapters.n: Jesus replies that Pilate has no power over him except what was granted from above. The one who handed him over bears the greater guilt.

f.w: except it were given thee from above
he that delivered me unto thee
f.g: Probably Caiaphas, who handed him to Pilate — or Judas, who betrayed him.

chapters.n: Pilate tries harder to release him, but the leaders play their trump card: free him and you’re no friend of Caesar. Anyone claiming to be king opposes the emperor.

f.g: “Friend of Caesar” could be an official honor; losing it — or being reported to the emperor Tiberius — could end Pilate’s career.

chapters.n: Pilate brings Jesus out and sits on the judgment seat at a place called the Stone Pavement, Gabbatha in Aramaic.

f.g: An Aramaic word probably meaning “elevated place.”
The official platform from which a Roman magistrate gave verdicts.

chapters.n: It is about noon on the day of preparation for Passover — the time Passover lambs were being slaughtered in the temple. Pilate presents Jesus: “Behold your King!”

f.g: John’s timing shows Jesus dying as the true Passover Lamb.
About noon, counting from sunrise.

chapters.n: The crowd cries, “Away with him!” When Pilate asks if he should crucify their King, the chief priests declare, “We have no king but Caesar” — a shocking rejection of God as Israel’s true King.

f.w: We have no king but Cæsar

chapters.n: Pilate hands Jesus over to be crucified, and the soldiers lead him away.
Carrying his own cross, Jesus goes out to the Place of the Skull — Golgotha in Aramaic, Calvary from the Latin.

f.g: Like Isaac carrying the wood up Moriah; the other Gospels add Simon of Cyrene was compelled to help.
Aramaic for “skull.” The Latin word calvaria gives us “Calvary.”

chapters.n: There they crucify him between two others, one on either side, with Jesus in the middle.
Pilate has a notice fastened to the cross: “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.” Crucified men usually had their crime posted.

f.g: title = a written notice or placard (Latin titulus).

chapters.n: Many people read it, since the site was near the city and the sign was written in Hebrew (Aramaic), Greek, and Latin — the languages of religion, culture, and empire. In effect, Christ was proclaimed King to the whole world.
The chief priests object and want it changed to say only that he claimed to be king.

f.w: Write not, The King of the Jews
f.g: They resent the public statement, which mocks them as much as Jesus.

chapters.n: Pilate refuses: “What I have written, I have written.” Without intending it, he leaves standing a true declaration.

f.w: What I have written I have written
f.g: A stubborn assertion of Roman authority.

chapters.n: The four soldiers divide his clothing among themselves. His tunic is seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom — some see a hint of the high priest’s robe.
Rather than tear the tunic, they gamble for it, fulfilling the Psalm: they divided his clothes and cast lots for his garment.

f.w: They parted my raiment among them

f.g: To throw marked stones or dice to decide something.

chapters.n: Near the cross stand faithful women: Jesus’s mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene. While most disciples have fled, these women remain.

f.g: From Magdala on the Sea of Galilee; Jesus had healed her.
Possibly Salome, mother of James and John (Mark 15:40; Matthew 27:56).

chapters.n: Seeing his mother and the beloved disciple nearby, Jesus says to her, “Woman, here is your son.” Even in agony he cares for his mother.

f.g: “Woman” was a respectful address.

chapters.n: To the disciple he says, “Here is your mother,” and from then on that disciple takes her into his home.

f.w: took her unto his own home
f.g: Joseph was likely dead by now, and Jesus’s brothers did not yet believe.

chapters.n: Knowing everything is now accomplished, Jesus says, “I thirst.” The one who offered living water experiences real human thirst, fulfilling scripture.
A jar of sour wine sits nearby; they soak a sponge in it, put it on a hyssop branch, and lift it to his lips.

f.g: Cheap sour wine, a common drink of soldiers.
Hyssop was used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb on the doorposts.

chapters.n: After drinking, Jesus says, “It is finished,” bows his head, and gives up his spirit. His work of atonement is complete; he chooses the moment of his death.

f.g: Greek tetelestai — “accomplished,” “paid in full.” The JST of Matthew records Jesus saying “Father, it is finished, thy will is done.”
ghost = spirit. He gave his life; it was not taken (John 10:18).

chapters.n: Because the next day was a special Sabbath — Passover week — the leaders didn’t want bodies left hanging. They ask Pilate to have the men’s legs broken to hasten death so the bodies could be removed.

f.g: A Sabbath that coincided with the Passover feast, especially sacred.

f.w: that the bodies should not remain upon the cross

chapters.n: The soldiers break the legs of the two men crucified with him. A crucified man pushed up on his legs to breathe; breaking them caused quick suffocation.

f.g: brake = broke.

chapters.n: But Jesus is already dead, so they don’t break his legs.

Instead a soldier thrusts a spear into his side, and blood and water flow out — evidence that he truly died. Many Christians have also seen in the blood and water symbols of atonement, baptism, and the sacrament.
John stresses that this comes from an eyewitness whose testimony is true, written so readers may believe.
These things fulfilled scripture: not one of his bones would be broken — just as no bone of the Passover lamb was to be broken.

f.w: A bone of him shall not be broken

chapters.n: Another scripture said they would look on the one they had pierced.

f.w: They shall look on him whom they pierced

chapters.n: Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple who had been afraid of the leaders, boldly asks Pilate for Jesus’s body. Pilate agrees, and Joseph takes it.

f.g: A wealthy member of the council who had not agreed to Jesus’s condemnation.

chapters.n: Nicodemus — who first came to Jesus by night — now comes openly, bringing about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes, a burial fit for a king.

f.g: A Roman pound was about 12 ounces, so roughly 75 modern pounds (34 kg) — a lavish amount.

chapters.n: They wrap his body in linen cloths with the spices, following Jewish burial custom.
Near the crucifixion site was a garden with a new tomb where no one had ever been laid. Life began in a garden, the Atonement began in a garden, and the Resurrection will happen in a garden.

f.g: sepulchre = tomb.

chapters.n: Because it was the day of preparation and the tomb was close by, they laid Jesus there before the Sabbath began at sundown.

f.w: the sepulchre was nigh at hand
f.g: nigh at hand = nearby.

chapters.n: Early Sunday morning, while still dark, Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb and finds the stone rolled away. The first day of the week would become the Christian day of worship because of this morning.

f.w: The first day of the week

chapters.n: She runs to Peter and the beloved disciple and tells them someone has taken the Lord’s body and she doesn’t know where. Her first thought is grave robbery, not resurrection.

f.w: we know not where they have laid him
f.g: “We” hints that other women were with her, as the other Gospels report.

chapters.n: Peter and the other disciple set out for the tomb.
They run together; the other disciple, probably younger, outruns Peter and arrives first.

f.g: An eyewitness detail, told with a touch of personal memory.

chapters.n: He bends down and peers in, seeing the linen burial cloths lying there, but doesn’t go in.

f.g: Rock-cut tomb entrances were often low, requiring one to stoop.

chapters.n: Peter arrives and goes straight in. He sees the linen cloths lying there.
He notices the face cloth folded and lying separately from the other wrappings. This is no hurried theft — robbers would not have unwrapped the body and left the cloths neatly behind.

f.w: the napkin, that was about his head
f.g: Unlike Lazarus, who came out still bound, Jesus left his grave clothes behind.

chapters.n: Then the beloved disciple goes in, sees, and believes — the first to believe in the Resurrection, even before seeing the risen Lord.
John explains that they still hadn’t understood the scriptures teaching that he must rise from the dead.

f.w: that he must rise again from the dead

chapters.n: The two disciples go back home.

f.g: Probably their lodging in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Mary stays outside the tomb, weeping. Through her tears she stoops to look inside.

f.w: Mary stood without at the sepulchre weeping
f.g: without = outside. Her loving persistence is about to be rewarded.

chapters.n: She sees two angels in white sitting where Jesus’s body had been, one at the head and one at the feet — perhaps recalling the two cherubim on either end of the mercy seat of the ark.
They ask why she is weeping. She explains they have taken her Lord away and she doesn’t know where.

f.g: A gentle question — there is no need to weep.

chapters.n: She turns and sees Jesus standing there but doesn’t recognize him.

f.w: knew not that it was Jesus

chapters.n: Jesus asks why she is weeping and whom she is looking for. Thinking he’s the gardener, she asks where he has put the body so she can take it.

f.w: supposing him to be the gardener
f.g: A touching irony — in a sense, he is the Gardener of new creation.

chapters.n: Jesus speaks her name: “Mary.” She recognizes him instantly and cries out “Rabboni!” — “my Teacher!” The Good Shepherd calls his sheep by name.

f.g: An Aramaic form of rabbi, more personal and affectionate: “my master/teacher.”

chapters.n: Jesus tells her not to cling to him, for he has not yet ascended to the Father. She is to tell his “brethren” that he ascends to “my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God.” Mary becomes the first witness of the risen Lord.

f.g: The JST reads “Hold me not.” Greek: “stop clinging to me.”

chapters.n: Mary goes to the disciples announcing, “I have seen the Lord!” and reports what he told her.

That Sunday evening the disciples gather behind locked doors, afraid of the authorities. Suddenly Jesus stands among them and says, “Peace be with you.” His resurrected body is real, yet not limited the way ours are.
He shows them his hands and side, proving it is truly he, crucified and now alive. Their fear gives way to joy.

f.w: he shewed unto them his hands and his side

chapters.n: Again he gives them peace, then commissions them: as the Father sent him, he now sends them.
He breathes on them and says, “Receive the Holy Ghost,” echoing God breathing life into Adam. The full outpouring would come at Pentecost.
He gives them priesthood authority to forgive or retain sins — the power to act in his name in matters of salvation.

f.g: remit = forgive, release.

chapters.n: Thomas, one of the Twelve, wasn’t there that evening.

f.g: “The Twin.”

chapters.n: The others tell him they have seen the Lord. Thomas says he won’t believe unless he sees and touches the nail wounds and the wound in his side. He wants the same evidence they had.
A week later, with Thomas present and the doors again locked, Jesus appears among them and greets them with peace.

f.g: Counted inclusively — the following Sunday.

chapters.n: Jesus invites Thomas to touch his hands and side, and urges him to stop doubting and believe. Jesus meets Thomas exactly where he is.
Thomas responds with the highest confession in the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!” The doubter becomes the one who declares Jesus’s divinity most plainly.
Jesus says Thomas believes because he has seen; blessed are those who believe without seeing. This blessing is for every later believer, including us.

f.w: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed

chapters.n: John admits that Jesus did many other signs in front of his disciples that aren’t recorded in this book.
John states the purpose of his whole Gospel: these things are written so readers may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name.
Later, back in Galilee, Jesus shows himself again to his disciples by the Sea of Tiberias. John now tells how it happened.

f.g: on this wise = in this way.

chapters.n: Seven disciples are together: Peter, Thomas, Nathanael from Cana, James and John (the sons of Zebedee), and two others.
Peter announces he’s going fishing, and the others join him. They work all night and catch nothing — just like the night before Jesus first called Peter.
At dawn Jesus stands on the beach, but the disciples don’t recognize him.

f.w: knew not that it was Jesus

chapters.n: He calls out affectionately, “Children, do you have any fish?” They answer, “No.”

f.g: A friendly term, like “lads” or “friends.”
meat = food; here, fish to eat.

chapters.n: He tells them to cast the net on the right side of the boat. They do — and the net is so full they can’t haul it in. Obeying his word brings abundance where their own effort failed.

f.w: Cast the net on the right side of the ship

chapters.n: The beloved disciple recognizes him first: “It is the Lord!” Impetuous Peter throws on his outer garment and jumps into the water to reach Jesus.

f.w: girt his fisher's coat unto him
f.g: He tied on his outer garment; “naked” here means stripped down to work clothes.

f.w: did cast himself into the sea

chapters.n: The others follow in the boat, about a hundred yards from shore, dragging the net full of fish.

f.g: A cubit was about 18 inches, so roughly 100 yards (90 meters).

chapters.n: On shore they find a charcoal fire with fish cooking on it and bread. Jesus has already prepared breakfast for them.

f.g: The only other charcoal fire in John is where Peter denied Jesus — the scene is set for his restoration.

chapters.n: Jesus asks them to bring some of the fish they’ve just caught. He includes their effort in the meal.

f.g: The Lord invites our contribution, even when he could supply everything.

chapters.n: Peter drags the net ashore — 153 large fish — and the net hasn’t torn. Many have seen the large catch as a symbol of the great harvest of souls the apostles would gather.

f.w: an hundred and fifty and three
f.g: A precise eyewitness count; ancient and modern readers have proposed many symbolic meanings, none certain.

f.w: yet was not the net broken

chapters.n: Jesus says, “Come and eat breakfast.” No one dares ask who he is — they know it is the Lord.

f.g: dine = eat a meal; here the morning meal.
durst = dared.

chapters.n: Jesus takes the bread and gives it to them, and the fish too — echoing the feeding of the five thousand by the same lake.
John notes this is the third time Jesus appeared to the disciples as a group after his resurrection.

After breakfast Jesus asks Peter, “Do you love me more than these?” — more than the other disciples do, or perhaps more than the boats and fish of his old life. Peter says yes. Jesus replies, “Feed my lambs.”

f.w: lovest thou me more than these?

chapters.n: A second time Jesus asks if Peter loves him, and Peter says yes. Jesus says, “Tend my sheep.”

f.g: Greek here is poimainō — shepherd, tend, care for — a slightly different verb than in verses 15 and 17.

chapters.n: A third time Jesus asks, and Peter is hurt. He answers, “Lord, you know everything; you know I love you.” Jesus says again, “Feed my sheep.” Three questions mirror three denials — a gentle, complete restoration.

f.g: In the first two questions Jesus uses agapaō; Peter answers with phileō. The third time Jesus uses Peter’s word. Many see significance in the shift, though the words overlap in meaning.

chapters.n: Jesus then foretells Peter’s future: when young, he dressed himself and went where he pleased; when old, he will stretch out his hands, and others will bind him and take him where he would not choose to go.

f.w: thou shalt stretch forth thy hands
f.g: Early Christian tradition holds that Peter was crucified in Rome.
girded = dressed oneself, tied one’s belt.

chapters.n: John explains that Jesus was indicating the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. Then Jesus tells him, “Follow me” — the same call he first heard by this lake.

f.w: by what death he should glorify God

chapters.n: Peter turns and sees the beloved disciple following — the one who leaned on Jesus at the Last Supper and asked who would betray him.

f.w: which also leaned on his breast at supper

chapters.n: Peter asks, “Lord, what about him?”

f.g: A natural question — but it shifts attention from Peter’s own calling.

chapters.n: Jesus answers: if he wants this disciple to remain until he returns, that’s not Peter’s concern. “You follow me.” Each disciple has their own path.

f.w: If I will that he tarry till I come
f.g: tarry = remain. Latter-day revelation teaches that John asked for and received power to remain on earth and bring souls to Christ until the Second Coming.

chapters.n: A rumor spread among believers that this disciple wouldn’t die. John corrects it: Jesus didn’t say that, only “If I want him to remain…” Latter-day Saints understand that John was translated — changed so as not to taste death until Christ’s return.
The author identifies himself as this disciple, the one who testifies of these things and wrote them down. Others add, “we know his testimony is true.”
John closes by saying that Jesus did so much more that if it were all written down, the world couldn’t hold the books. Christ’s life and works are beyond full telling.

f.w: the world itself could not contain the books
